#170550. Are You Ready for the ’80s Fashion Revival?

Are You Ready for the ’80s Fashion Revival?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It happened suddenly: golden shades, huge shoulders, stacks of oversize jewelry.
  • In a recent development, and why not?
  • The obsession has already started (or, rather, it never really ended) in the vintage world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It happened suddenly: golden shades, huge shoulders, stacks of oversize jewelry. At Anthony Vaccarello’s swan song for Saint Laurent, it was all golden with big jackets, safari suits, and joyfully ruffled blouses fit for a Joan Collins-era Dynasty, but built for 2026. For spring/summer 2027, the ’80s have been a big focus. Valentino showcased jewel-toned gowns with piled-on maximalist pearls, and Giorgio Armani’s strong shoulders were straight out of a fashion history book. Mugler and Calvin Klein did strong silhouettes that alluded to the era. And even Louis Vuitton couldn’t help but look back to Upcoming York in the 1980s for its recent cruise collection, presenting models in stiff jeans and Keith Haring tops.

In a recent development, and why not? The ’80s were a time of experimentalism and personality, making it ripe to be mined for fashion inspiration and also less referenced than the forever hall of famer ’90s and Y2K style that fashion can’t stop loving.

The obsession has already started (or, rather, it never really ended) in the vintage world. Haile Lidow, founder of Lidow Archive, has seen a demand recently for her vintage drop waists and ruffle-skirt dresses in wild patterns. “I have so many in my collection that have gone neglected for years and are finally being noticed,” she tells ELLE. “Also, the ’80s power suits! They are back! Sometimes I update the skirt length if it feels too dated. We call it ‘minify’ but regardless, the requests for these are pouring in.”.

Sources indicate that for some, it’s about nostalgia, but for others, it’s totally latest. Violet Sky, a 26-year-old Gen Z singer first became inspired to dress totally ’80s after watching the film Girls Just Want to Have Fun while she was in high school. “It was all the bright colors and just how fun everything was and the significant hair,” she tells ELLE. “I just felt really drawn to it. I didn’t really have my own personal style, and so at that moment, I was like, well, why don’t I just explore this?” She started by pulling pieces from her mother and grandmother’s old wardrobe in her attic, and now exclusively wears acid-wash denim, tops bedazzled with rhinestones, and Reebok Classics every day.

“I think fashion, and interiors, and so many other aesthetic-based industries has been stuck in a really boring rut that’s been disguised as minimalism,” adds Lidow. “It started in the late ’90s as ‘chic’ and developed into an excuse for society to try less. The ’80s were the opposite: one bangle was never enough, you had to have four. Eyelids were splashed in bright colors and patterns were clashing all over the place. I think we’ve finally grown bored of the boring. We want to have fun again.”.

Even fashion historians can’t help but think of the ’80s as a sort of golden age of fashion, when Vivienne Westwood and Christian Lacroix were sending highly creative pieces down the runway. Valerie Steele, director and chief curator of The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology, even associates the era with a shoe renaissance, which we’ve also been experiencing in 2026 with the rise of It shoes. “I think what we’re seeing in part may be a hope that we can come back to a period when fashion really was fashionable, because now we’re seeing so much dissatisfaction with fashion, and with the costs of fashion, not only personally, but also to the environment, and to workers and so on,” she tells ELLE.

The familiar feeling of power dressing in the air (and on the runways) with these ’80s silhouettes is deeply tied to the female gaze. “What you see in the ’80s is that it’s coming out of a feminist movement that was growing in the ’70s, and then in the ’80s became a somewhat different feminist movement, so it was more kind of, girly, economic feminism rather than a sort of leftist, ideological feminism of the ’70s,” adds Steele. “So instead of working-class androgyny, you had suits like men had. You had powerful shoulders, you had a look of Amazonian femininity going down the runway, and that resonated with a kind of booming market, and a period when maybe, maybe feminism was becoming more commodified, or that was certainly a period when people realized that they could market specifically to women by having things that look both powerful and sexy.” Who can argue with that?

According to recent reports, “I think that bright colors and loud fashion of the ’80s is something that’s so opposite than what’s kind of like going on today at least in everyone’s everyday life versus the runway,” adds Sky. “People are kind of intrigued about that. And they want to maybe try something different.” The ’80s revival may be nostalgic, but its appeal feels entirely of the moment: it’s instant personality in an era of sameness.

The Scoop with Kolor’s Taro Horiuchi: On His Zara Collab

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week.
  • It has been revealed that this week’s guest is Taro Horiuchi, who took over the creative direction of Japanese brand Kolor from its founder Junichi Abe, a couple of years ago.
  • Before all that, Taro studied photography at London’s Kingston University and fashion design at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, alongside Demna and Glenn Martens, who were in the year above and below, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

It has been revealed that this week’s guest is Taro Horiuchi, who took over the creative direction of Japanese brand Kolor from its founder Junichi Abe, a couple of years ago. Before that, Taro was running his namesake womenswear label, which he launched after moving to France in 2010, as well as a menswear line called TH Product, founded in 2018 (the two merged when he took over Kolor in 2025).

Before all that, Taro studied photography at London’s Kingston University and fashion design at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, alongside Demna and Glenn Martens, who were in the year above and below, respectively. The thread that seems to bind Taro’s work together is turning basic garments on their heads, which is also what he sought to do in his most recent collaboration with a little conglomerate called Zara. I called him up to discuss that and more.

Recent findings suggest that on December 3, we will be launching a collaboration with Zara. We are hosting a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2, and the global launch will be the following day. It’s the first global collaboration we’ve confirmed since I took over as creative director in 2025, so I feel honored to be in this position. The collection will span womenswear, menswear, and childrenswear. It’s the first time Kolor is making kids’ clothing, so that was an interesting challenge for us.

Shots from the Kolor x Zara campaign. It’s the brand’s first global collaboration since Horiuchi took over as creative director from founder Junichi Abe in 2025.

What was it like designing children’s clothes then?

According to recent reports, the core challenge for us in this project was expressing the brand without the high pricing and intricate details. We wanted to make good, interesting clothes regardless of whether it was for children or adults. However, there are constraints when it comes to making clothes for children, both in terms of the textiles you can use and because the accessories and the parts on the clothing are very small. That was definitely a learning experience for us, which we took on happily.

Recent findings suggest that can you tell me a little bit about the collection? What was the inspiration behind it?

So the theme for this project is “World Uniform”. It’s something we do at Kolor: take something basic and turn it into something a little different. Fans of Kolor are always on the cutting edge of fashion, and they are always seeking something new. But those who shop at Zara are looking for clothes for their daily lives. So our challenge was to find the perfect balance between familiar and inspirational.

Sources indicate that behind the scenes of the Kolor x Zara campaign shoot. The collection’s theme, “World Uniform”, reflects Kolor’s habit of taking basic garments and making them “a little different”.

For sure, there are those who go to Zara for basics, but I’d argue that’s changing because of all the luxury brand collaborations Zara orchestrates, including the one with Kolor.

It has been revealed that one thing that really stood out to me through this experience was the very high quality of fabrics and operations that Zara offers. My family and friends wear a lot of Zara, though I personally haven’t, so I wasn’t aware of the way they work. But the whole process was very inspirational to me. Both the product quality and the speed of responding were quite remarkable.

I remember when Zara rolled out in Greece; I was about 8 or 9. My mother was delighted because she could buy cheap but nice clothes for us. I still have some of those sweaters from 30 years ago, and my son wears them now. Has it been fun to work with Zara’s manufacturing resources?

In a recent development, for sure. When it comes to any collaboration, it doesn’t make sense for me to make anything you can make alone. I am very happy to say we managed to realize something that Kolor couldn’t have made on its own, and I believe Zara feels the same way about us.

A look from Kolor x Zara, which releases globally on December 3 after a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2.

Industry observers note that you’ve taken over Kolor from its founder. It feels like a tough gig to follow a founder who is still involved and alive. But if we look at people like Julian Klausner at Dries Van Noten and Haider Ackermann at Tom Ford, maybe that’s part of the success recipe? How do you work with Junichi Abe, and is there a lot of pressure to match him?

I’ll answer your second question about pressure first. Of course, I feel the pressure, and I also respect Abe-san incredibly. Whether it’s a recipe for success, I’m not sure yet. What I can say is that the core value and DNA of a fashion brand aren’t something you can build in one day. It takes time. All I can do is what Abe-san told me to do at the very beginning of my time at Kolor: “Don’t repeat what I could. Just make Kolor unique to you,” he said.

It has been revealed that there are quite a few open positions at the significant luxury houses at the moment, and we expect them to be filled any day now. Does the constant change-up in creative directors affect the way you and other designers work or view the industry?

According to recent reports, things change much faster than when I started in fashion around maybe 2005. As I was saying earlier, building a brand takes time because it needs to have a culture and a philosophy. The compatibility of the brand and the designer is very notable too in all that. In that sense, speedy changes are not good because they don’t allow the two to get to know each other.

Kolor x Zara. Horiuchi states the collaboration let him make something Kolor “couldn’t have made on its own”, thanks to Zara’s fabrics and production speed.

Applications for the 2027 LVMH prize are now open. You won the Diesel Award at ITS 20 years ago. How necessary are those awards and prizes to young designers?

I graduated from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp in 2007, and I am still so thankful to Barbara (Franchin, founder and director of ITS) and Renzo (Rosso, founder of Diesel and founder and chairman of OTB) for the opportunity. Looking back now, this was a big turning point in my career. It wasn’t so much about winning the award, but more about the people I met. Demna was in the year above me at Antwerp, and together we organized an exhibition about Japan. At the Diesel award, I met Matthieu Blazy, who is now at Chanel. So, for me, those prizes and competitions are meaningful because of the communities they draw together. If you want to tell what the future of the industry will be in 20 years, you should look at who is entering those competitions now.

Industry observers note that but I have a concern about the future of the industry. When I was a student, the tuition fees for Antwerp were around €1,000 per year. Now, for non-EEA students, it’s between €13,000 and €25,000. The people who can’t afford such high tuition will not be entering the fashion industry. Demna wouldn’t have been at Antwerp if the tuition was any more expensive. So maybe, one suggestion for the organizations that support those awards would be to focus more on scholarships and grants.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

It has been revealed that A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

It has been revealed that using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

Vintage Watch Experts Break Down Their 6 Favorite Timepieces

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And another thing, a watch collector might say as they try to sell you on the virtues of the hobby, is that you can bring them anywhere.
  • Last September, Fisk was at the Waldorf Astoria in Newly introduced York when he spotted a collector wearing the coveted 1940s Longines model known as the “Tre Tacche.” Watches are challenging subjects even in a photo studio, but Fisk was forced to stumble around the hotel bar looking for any slice of decent lighting to capture the Longines before it slipped through his fingers forever.
  • It has been revealed that “You meet someone who just happens to be wearing something really special on the wrist that day, and you have to just be ready for it,” Fisk tells me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And another thing, a watch collector might say as they try to sell you on the virtues of the hobby, is that you can bring them anywhere. Unlike other high-value collectibles—cars or paintings, say—you can wear even the rarest of grail-worthy timepieces to, say, a dimly lit bar. Which is precisely where James Fisk—the photographer behind the images in the just-released Vintage Watches: The Modern Guide, written by the renowned dealers Eric Wind and Charlie Dunne—encountered one of the most historic tickers in the book.

Last September, Fisk was at the Waldorf Astoria in Newly introduced York when he spotted a collector wearing the coveted 1940s Longines model known as the “Tre Tacche.” Watches are challenging subjects even in a photo studio, but Fisk was forced to stumble around the hotel bar looking for any slice of decent lighting to capture the Longines before it slipped through his fingers forever. Used to working on the fly, the photographer keeps 40 or so fabric swatches with him at all times, just in case he needs to lay a watch on top of one as a backdrop for an impromptu shoot.

It has been revealed that “You meet someone who just happens to be wearing something really special on the wrist that day, and you have to just be ready for it,” Fisk tells me. It’s how many of the legendary vintage watches—mildly key subjects for a book on the topic—ended up in Wind and Dunne’s newly introduced tome.

The book is a comprehensive deep dive into the booming world of vintage watch collecting. Wind and Dunne take readers on a Jungle Cruise-style tour of this sometimes daunting hobby: On your left are the questions that all newcomers should know to ask before buying a vintage watch; on your right, you’ll find testimonies from famous collectors like David Chang, Ronny Chieng, and Daniel Dae Kim; straight ahead are dispatches on the most notable brands, from Rolex to Piaget.

According to recent reports, vintage Watches: The Modern Guide is designed to be as welcoming and accessible as possible. While many watch volumes sell for hundreds of dollars, Dunne and Wind made it a point to price theirs at $60 (or $50 on Amazon right now). “A lot of people will be able to afford this book,” Dunne states. “And then, hopefully, they’ll aspire to get some of the watches in it and it’ll ignite their interest in the hobby.”.

Below are Wind and Dunne’s favorite selections from the book, including one that the latter was most insistent on including to represent the more affordable side of the spectrum.

It has been revealed that there may be two six-figure watches on the cover, but flip just a few pages into the book and you’ll find this delightful little example from Fortis. “I forced Eric to put that in,” Dunne jokes. “He said, ‘We're not putting that in—it's too cheap!” The watch sells for just a touch over $1,000, and this exact piece was in Wind’s collection for several years. He calls it a personal favorite from his years of collecting.

The Shipman might not be historically crucial or carry great provenance, but it serves an important dimension in the book as a representative for the many types of pieces that comprise a true collection. “Not only [does it show] the range of what is out there as far as exceptional watches at all price points, but also it's one of the most fun and quirky watches in the book,” Dunne states. “You want to have very, very serious watches in your collection, but you also want to have things that put a smile on your face at any price point.”.

How do you choose the cover stars for a book about vintage watches? You start with the obvious: The Rolex “Paul Newman” Daytona (bottom) is the poster boy for vintage collecting. The famed Phillips auctioneer Aurel Bacs, who sold the actor’s personal version for a record $17.8 million, calls Newman wearing this special variant “the Adam and Eve moment in Rolex collecting.”.

Industry observers note that but the Daytona’s partner on the cover, the Audemars Piguet ref. 5516, is an unexpected choice that packs just as much historical heft. “This is one of the most notable watches ever made, because of the leap year indicator” Wind notes. “AP beat Patek by over 20 years to have a leap year indicator on the bottom. This and the Royal Oak are probably two of the greatest impacts on the Swiss watch industry.” Only nine were made, and Wind sold this example for $545,000 while he was at Christie’s in 2015. I love the specificity of the watch’s leap-year function, which only comes into play once every four years.

Industry observers note that wind and Dunne are longtime evangelists for the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch in the late ’40s and early ’50s. This particular reference is modified to include a tide indicator at the 9 o’clock subdial, done up in extremely pretty tones of sandy tan and deep sea blue. The example featured in the book remains pristine—with a perfect eggshell-white dial—thanks to the original owner stuffing it in a drawer unworn for decades. The watch got to Wind by way of a friend, whom he sent to fetch it from a diner in the original owner’s home state of Arizona.

The watch that Fisk scrambled to shoot in a hotel bar was well worth the hustle. “Longines, in some sense, was Rolex before Rolex,” Wind claims. The brand was “the tool watch manufacturer in the 1930s and 1940s, particularly with their Tre Tacche cases. Many of the great aviators and pioneers of the time wore Longines watches.” The model gets its nickname from the three notches on the caseback that helped watchmakers screw the case together tighter to prevent water and dust from getting inside.

Sources indicate that this is a classic watch—a defining example of a dress model—done up with a particularly sleek dial. Patek Philippe made endless examples of the 96, allowing collectors to select their favorite flavor from the lot. Wind and Dunne sold this example but both wish they could have it back. “ I don't think it's coming to the light ever,” Dunne laments.

To capture the glossy black dial in the book, Fisk shot the watch at two different angles to mimic the experience of tilting it back and forth in your hands.

In a recent development, the very last watch added to the book was this version of the GMT-Master, one of the Crown’s most important models. The ref. 1675 isn’t the first GMT-Master that Rolex made, but it’s considered the platonic ideal visually and the most collectible among vintage watch lovers. Its predecessors featured troublesome bezels that were prone to cracking, as well as poisonous amounts of radium.

The 1675 was produced for just over 20 years, from 1959 to 1980. This one belongs to Fisk and was on his wrist when we met last week. “We got this right as the pages were printed,” Dunne claims, “and we started yelling in emails [to the publisher] saying, ‘We have to stop everything. Put this page in there.’”.

#170544. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va.
  • The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.
  • Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Recent findings suggest that rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

Recent findings suggest that “Yes, absolutely,” she mentioned when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, mentioned she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses revealed a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack mentioned she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

Industry observers note that “That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this glitch.”.

Leger Fernández remarked if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

According to recent reports, “We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández stated. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

#170543. The Best Japanese Restaurants in London, From Omakase Counters to Neighborhood Gems

The Best Japanese Restaurants in London, From Omakase Counters to Neighborhood Gems

📅 29 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles.
  • Industry observers note that but in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou.
  • From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles. (No piece of sushi has ever needed gold leaf so liberally applied.) Historically, to eat well, you’ve had to splurge: it isn’t cheap, after all, to source top-quality fish in the British capital, and it’s still worth saving your pennies for a blowout meal at one of the city’s top omakase counters, such as Sushi Kanesaka or Sushi Tetsu.

Industry observers note that but in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou. (Its former location next to the old Condé Nast offices on Hanover Square led it to be nicknamed the “Vogue canteen.”) And that’s without mentioning beloved neighborhood spots like Uchi Hackney or Jin Kichi in Hampstead.

From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.

Located within the ritzy 45 Park Lane hotel, this Michelin-starred, omakase-only destination with 13 seats is as atmospheric a sushi experience as you’ll find anywhere in London. Step through the discreet noren curtain that marks the entrance, and you’ll feel as if you entered a portal straight to Kyoto, with the gently lit interiors—all hinoki wood, lime plaster walls, and intricate kumiko lattice work—serving as a delicate backdrop for the equally delicate flight of dishes that follows. Helmed by legendary chef Shinji Kanesaka, the 13-seat restaurant offers a masterclass in traditional Edomae-style omakase using an impressive array of locally sourced ingredients: a silky pot of chawanmushi topped with the briny sweetness of fresh Cornish crab; marbled, melt-in-your-mouth fatty tuna nigiri with perfectly seasoned rice sourced from Japan’s Yamagata Prefecture; a Scottish lobster presented on a board then whizzed up into shatteringly crisp morsels of tempura. With a price tag of £420 per person, it isn’t for the faint of heart—but for those seeking true perfection, it’s London’s ultimate bucket-list sushi destination. —Liam Hess.

A true Mayfair stalwart, Kiku has been serving the neighborhood since 1978, making it one of the oldest Japanese restaurants in the city—and unlike some of its flashier neighboring sushi restaurants, Kiku’s vibe is one of calm, quiet elegance. It’s the place to go for a consistently excellent, no-frills sushi experience where the quality of the fish speaks for itself, whether it’s the salmon and tuna in a classic sashimi set, or rare delicacies like Hokkaido sea urchin and sweet prawn served on perfectly seasoned rice. The tempura here is world-class, with a light, lace-like batter, and the £40 lunchtime set menu—which consists of yakitori, tempura, sushi, miso soup, and a dessert—is one of the best deals in central London. The ultimate seal of approval? It’s a favorite spot among the staff at the nearby Japanese Embassy on Piccadilly. —L.H.

Sources indicate that this low-key but stylish joint, which opened in 2024 in a bijou shopfront on Brewer Street, is the brainchild of chef Takamasa Mogi—also the founder of popular Mayfair spot Cubé—and serves up astonishingly good sushi to the 10 seats that surround its subdued but stylish hinoki wood counter. (Soho regulars will remember the building’s former life as a manga store and karaoke bar—it turns out there’s still a karaoke room downstairs if your omakase dinner ends up getting a little raucous.) I was especially impressed by the creative but not overdone nigiri, including smoky slivers of seared Korean turbot and Spanish tuna with Oscietra caviar, served atop pillowy beds of red vinegar-seasoned rice. Given the quality, it’s excellent value too: the lunchtime menu offers salad, seven pieces of omakase nigiri, and dessert for £51.80, while the dinner menu of two appetizers, nine pieces of omakase nigiri, a temaki roll, and dessert comes to £89. (They also do a well-priced pre-theater menu if you’re planning to catch a West End show.) —L.H.

Under former Noma sommelier Yuki Kaneko’s ownership, Yuki Bar has transcended East London’s small plates and orange wine scene. Within the low-lit, 20-cover spot soundtracked by disco J-pop, dishes riff on French and Nordic classics with Japanese inflections, like a sesame-studded take on oeufs mayonnaise, embracing home-style cooking and a choose-your-own-adventure menu of “snacks, littles, and larges.” A few portions of house-made potato crisps with sansho pepper and grilled onigiri kick the evening off, while rotating mains have included an aromatic chicken hot pot and blushing strips of beef tataki silken with soy sauce and mustard. Go with a group, be greedy, and get a few bottles recommended by Kaneko. —Anna Cafolla.

Sources indicate that mayfair isn’t exactly short on high-end sushi counters, so it takes serious pedigree to make a splashy entrance here. One of the few people capable of that is Shogo Amamoto, the Fukuoka-born chef behind Taipei’s two-Michelin-starred Sushi Amamoto—a reservation so notoriously tough to secure that die-hard sushi-heads are known to initiative trips to Taiwan around it. (Sushi mastery clearly runs in the family: his brother, Masamichi, helms Tokyo’s cult-favorite Higashiazabu Amamoto.) Chef Shogo’s London outpost forgoes the usual Mayfair glitz in favor of a serene, minimalist room centered around a pale hinoki wood counter and bespoke Japanese ceramics, and the focus lies firmly in classic Edomae culinary craft. Dishes feature top-tier seafood flown in from Tokyo’s Toyosu Market alongside standout European catches—translucent slices of French wild seabass sashimi with shiso flower and ponzu, a sweet seared Orkney scallop wrapped in crisp nori, or rich, smoky nodoguro whose skin crackles straight off the grill—and warm, perfectly seasoned rice. It’s purist without feeling oppressively solemn—and one of the freshest (in every sense) upcoming additions to London’s luxury sushi roster. —L.H.

Sources indicate that one of London’s sexiest counter seats (and that’s saying something), Ushio arrives from Fukuoka, on Japan’s Kyushu island. Its first European location, Ushio serves A5 wagyu omakase style (no sushi here!), specifically akami wagyu that has been imported from Japan. It’s leaner and higher in protein, with a taste that will unfurl across an incisive multi-course menu of wagyu every which way. You’ll get a card that tells you which prime cut of beef you’re eating with every course, and it’s certainly a journey. Some are barely kissed by the grill, others draped in a rich sukiyaki marinade or glazed in their signature tare sauce. A trio of tenderloin, tongue, and kurimi are delicately salted and presented gloriously as is. (My tip? Say yes to the extra curry course! If it wasn’t so sophisticated in there, I would be licking the bowl. Add the sake pairing and enjoy your time with the very charming sommelier too.) Finish with a (meatless, but still mighty) matcha choux puff. In a quiet, darkened corridor of Fitzrovia, the minimal interiors are stunning and sleek, just like the Fukuoka flagship, built around wood and stone with Ko-Imari porcelains and hand-built ceramics by Taeko Kajihara. And everyone who works there just seems cool! A spot that lingers long on the palate. —A.C.

Tucked behind a bright white storefront in Clerkenwell, this seven-person omakase experience is among the city’s toughest reservations to secure. Husband-and-wife duo Harumi and Toru Takahashi are behind the operation (the latter being the chef), both of whom are famously warm and welcoming, fostering a convivial atmosphere versus the buttoned-up formality of traditional omakase settings. The seasonal menu relies on what is strongest in the market that day, but expect sushi so fresh it melts in your mouth and impeccable sake pairings. The restaurant sits along Jerusalem Passage, an 18th-century path to the priory of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, which later transformed into a pedestrian walkway linking St John’s Square to Aylesbury Street. —Nicole Kliest.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re craving sushi but aren’t in the mood for a formal omakase environment, Uchi Hackney achieves an exceptional balance. This ultra-cozy spot in a residential area of Hackney leans on traditional Japanese design motifs (linen, ceramics, wood), and even encourages guests to kick off their shoes and slip into a pair of provided slippers. The restaurant began as a delivery service in 2015 and now offers a high-quality menu in its brick-and-mortar location, serving both brunch and dinner. As for the dishes, expect a variety of hot favorites such as grilled pork belly skewers and lightly deep-fried tofu, and savor the selection of fresh sushi and sake to round out the experience. (An aside: Uchi Hackney’s intimate ambience makes for the perfect date night locale.) —N.K.

Set on the ninth-floor Liverpool Street branch of Los Mochis, arriving at Luna Omakase comes with a delightful sense of ceremony. As the evening begins, you’ll be guided with your group from the bar along a nondescript corridor to a set of sliding doors that are opened—with plenty of theatrical flourish—to reveal the 12-seater dining room, where a sculptural timber counter is lit with a lunar glow against a backdrop of glittering skyline views of the City. Over the course of 12 seasonal plates, the vibe is lively and conversational, as the sushi masters hand each pristine slice of aged fish—think melt-in-your-mouth otoro tartare with Oscietra caviar served with a cloud of smoke, or juicy king crab leg nigiri with feathery shavings of yuzu—and artfully balance traditional technique and off-the-cuff flourishes throughout the meal. (If you fancy it, you can also make the evening more spirited—quite literally—courtesy of the tightly curated list of rare sakes and Japanese whiskies that the team is more than happy to geek out over, and that will serve as an instant conversation starter with your fellow sushi obsessives.) It’s intimate and undeniably stylish, but free of the stuffiness that can make your typical high-end omakase experience feel a little intimidating. —L.H.

In operation for nearly 30 years, this beloved sushi institution now operates across eight outposts in London (plus six in Tokyo). For those who favor great value and generous portion sizes, this restaurant chain consistently gets top marks. Choose from a menu of sushi, sashimi, nigiri, chirashi, unagi, or opt for a bento box to get the full experience. Their latest creation worth dining out for? Wagyu with black tobiko (or a ‘sushi taco’, as it’s so nicknamed). —N.K.

This Japanese udon noodle bar opened its doors in Soho back in 2010 and has since expanded to three popular London locations, plus a shop offering provisions such as chilli oil and jars of Fukujinzuke. The original location is worth a visit for the freshly made noodles and dashi alone, but don’t sleep on the weekly blackboard specials either (previous highlights include grilled corn with miso butter and fried whitebait with shibazuke cucumber). Koya Soho is walk-ins only and is open from breakfast through to dinner. —N.K.

This is where you go when you want authentic Japanese food and a killer sake selection, all in a calm, relaxed setting. Chisou’s two central London locations—Mayfair and Knightsbridge—treat guests to seasonally changing dishes and a menu of wow-worthy raw fish, with the option to sit at a sushi bar or at an intimate table. And back to the sake for a moment: Chisou prides itself on having one of the largest menus around, with experts on hand to suggest pairings and special events like sake and British cheese pairing classes led by specialists. —N.K.

It has been revealed that A charming, intimate spot tucked away on Newly introduced Quebec Street in Marylebone, Roketsu recently relaunched as a rare example in London of kappo-style dining, where the chefs will whip up a customized set menu based on a conversation about your preferences at the beginning of the meal. The team of chefs here take a creative approach to classic Japanese cuisine, folding in a handful of French flourishes: most notably, perhaps, with one of the restaurant’s signature dishes, an opening bite of a crisp wafer filled with 10-day miso-marinated foie gras. (Other highlights included Cornish cod with a vibrant nori sauce, and flame-grilled wagyu beef with yuzu oroshi for a clean, citrus-forward finish.) With an open kitchen behind a hinoki wood counter, Roketsu is an elevated, classically Japanese dining experience—but it also comes with an element of choose-your-own-adventure fun that makes it feel genuinely unique. —L.H.

If you’re seeking a quirkier spin on omakase dining, head over to Notting Hill, where you’ll find the six-seat Juno hidden in a speakeasy-like space at the back of Los Mochis, the popular neighborhood Mexican-Japanese restaurant on Uxbridge St. The dining room’s delightfully funky, “Tokyo-meets-Tulum” decor—bamboo, seagrass, high-gloss wallpaper—should serve as an initial clue for what to expect here: the textures and flavors of Japanese cuisine are lent a fresh twist courtesy of a bold, Mexican-inspired toolkit of spices, acids, and smoke. (Think chutoro spiked with a sharp kick of fermented jalapeño, or red bream brushed with lime aioli and topped with a sprinkle of crushed-up Oaxacan flying ant for a surprisingly delicious note of nutty earthiness.) Bring your friends and make it a party. —L.H.

There are few more scenic spots for lunchtime sushi in London than chef Endo Kazutoshi’s rooftop restaurant, which sits proudly above the Raffles London hotel at the Old War Office—and trades the monastic restraint of Endo’s Michelin-starred White City flagship for sweeping views over Horse Guards Parade. Grab an outdoor table and browse a menu that bridges Japanese precision with Mediterranean flourishes, the latter a direct nod to the years Kazutoshi spent cooking in Spain. Most of the dishes are built for sharing, so order generously: try the tuna tartare on miso brioche, the yellowfin tuna “chorizo” (its smoky, paprika-laced punch is balanced by pickled tsukemono and warm pita), or the charred, melt-in-the-mouth octopus with miso, fava beans, and asakura sansho—it’s all rather decadent, but somehow never overly heavy. Come for the pristine, perfectly seasoned nigiri; stay for the golden-hour sunset over the Neoclassical rooftops of this stately corner of central London. —L.H.

In a recent development, many of the best Japanese restaurants fall into two categories: no-frills neighborhood ramen and udon spots, or the kind of hushed, six-seater omakase counters where you might be frowned at for asking for extra soy sauce. Aki London, tucked inside a soaring, Grade II-listed former bank on Cavendish Square, couldn’t be more different. Designed by Francis Sultana, the dining room is all about pure, flamboyant glamour—think fluted marble columns, soaring coffered ceilings, and plush velvet banquette seating. This isn’t a case of style over substance, however: The kitchen leans into farm-to-table Japanese cooking rooted in Kyoto traditions, ranging from crisp, featherlight tempura rock shrimp to delicate steamed-and-crisped wagyu gyoza, to smoky, tare-brushed chicken thigh skewers straight off the robata grill. Whether you’re coming for a leisurely lunch or a late-night dinner, make sure to check out the subterranean cocktail bar first for a round of yuzu-infused martinis. (Aki is best enjoyed in the tech giant of a lively group.) —L.H.

A neighborhood restaurant in the truest sense, Jin Kichi’s cult following makes booking a table a competitive sport. This tiny, two-floor restaurant is cozy, often crowded, and wonderfully authentic. While the yakitori is a major draw, the sushi and sashimi are of a quality that rivals the city’s most expensive counters. It’s the kind of place where the chefs know the regulars by name (and where mentioned regulars might be the likes of Kate Moss and Harry Styles). —L.H.

#170541. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (430 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation.
  • More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.
  • extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Recent findings suggest that combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Industry observers note that add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

Latest Update: Every David Fincher Killer, Definitively Ranked

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Fincher is a rare breed of chameleonic auteur. In the past 40 years, he's directed music videos, commercials, feature films, and television series, all of which keep garnering more cultural importance, either immediately or in retrospect (hey, look, David Fincher directed a 1987 video for a single from a random Philly bar rock band!) Fincher is known for his technical prowess, his “impossible eye,” and his pioneering mastery of digital technology. He’s made love letters to old Hollywood, ripped-from-the-headlines tech-industry autopsies that render depositions as white-knuckle suspense, and popcorn home-invasion flicks. He’s taken turns at IP-franchise stewardship, adapted bestselling airport paperbacks, and told the oddly touching story of a mild-mannered, even-tempered gentleman from Newly introduced Orleans who ages backwards. But if Fincher has a career throughline, a raison d’etre, it’s his pursuit and depiction of killers—a focus made quite overt in The Killer, a fascinating and highly meta film which hits Netflix Friday after a limited theatrical run over the past two weeks.

Recent findings suggest that in Fincher's films, killers—particularly serial killers—provide an extreme window into human nature. They are symptoms of a sick society, prophets, self-appointed Gods and monsters, blank canvases for us to project our conspiracies and insecurities onto, or would-be celebrities killing for attention from a sensation-hungry media that's all too happy to give it to them. In the pale light of day or the fluorescent light of a prison visiting area, they're often sad, awkward misfits who understand themselves and their actions even less than we do. But by necessity, they're also methodical people who must put a great deal of thought and care into their grisly work in order to continue working. In this way, Fincher sees them as the equivalent of process-mad directors, blocking their victims and staging their crime scenes before selling them to a confused but riveted public.

In a recent development, time and time again, across his filmography, the image most associated with Fincher is the killer— or the hapless detectives pursuing them—shot from below, almost swallowed whole by a monochromatic backdrop that looms both far above and far behind them, dimly but immaculately lit, and bathed in shadow, inside Fincher's uncommonly steady, all-seeing and all-knowing frame. The killer’s maniacal focus, their certitude, is ours. The detective’s confusion—their understanding that they’re a step behind and a beat late, that they will never get the satisfying answers, the closure they’re looking for—is ours, too.

So for art, and for fun, let’s evaluate the many killers who've made Fincher's body of work as incredible and indelible as it is, based on a shifting, subjective equation of quality, efficacy, body count, and how they’re represented by the auteur himself.

Recent findings suggest that 23. The Narrator, Fight Club (1999).

Fight Club is a satire about bereft ineffectual masculinity, about neutered men crushed under Ikea catalogs, about eighth-grade-boy-level rebellion against materialism, capitalism, and every societal convention that places value on anything except chiseled abs, skinned knuckles, bullshit patter, and rugged individualism.

The “kill” here is committed by Edward Norton, as a character identified in the credits as “The Narrator” who murders Tyler Durden—his child, his liberator, his tormentor, and his imaginary friend—by, uh, shooting the side of his mouth, sort of? Somehow, the famously meticulous Fincher lands on a resolution that makes absolutely no sense according to the laws of physical interaction between The Narrator and Tyler Durden established within the rest of the film. Why does this apparition, who knows everything the narrator knows, and can punch The Narrator, can harm him physically without receiving the impact of those assaults, and can’t even be hit by The Narrator, die with his brains blown out as a result of his alter ego shooting off a chunk of his jaw? This is, hands down, the worst “kill” in the Fincher filmography.

According to recent reports, 22. The Random Guy Who Kills Madonna, “Bad Girl” (1993).

According to recent reports, fincher did his most vital music video work for his muse and rumored paramour Madonna, who tapped him to direct videos for hits like “Vogue” and “Express Yourself.” But one of their less heralded collaborations was this bizarre minor work, a video (for a song from Erotica) that plays like a dumbed-down Wings of Desire. Madonna is a stressed-out high-achieving corporate type who unwinds by making bad and eventually fatal decisions. After her Bruno Ganz-like guardian angel (Christopher Walken) makes out with her, she pursues sex with a hookup who clearly intends to murder her. We only see the killer from Madonna's POV, and when he kills her it's presented as her choice, rather than the result of any kind of premeditated plot by the killer; he's more of a prop than a person.

21. Weyland-Yutani Employee, Alien3 (1992).

For a filmmaker who so regularly trades in death, Fincher has depicted shockingly few frivolous ones. Nearly every kill in his work is personal and meaningful. But this is an exception. Towards the end of Alien3 , a commando representing the wantonly evil corporation smokes Francis Aaron, one of the COs on the prison planet Ripley has crash-landed on. The scene underscores the cynical ruthlessness of the outfit, but ultimately it’s just a faceless grunt shooting a stranger.

Industry observers note that 20. The Security Guard, Fight Club (1999).

In the act of executing Operation Latte Thunder, an ingenious plan to weaponize a piece of corporate art mounted in an office park fountain to destroy a franchise coffee shop in the lobby of a nearby building, Robert Paulson (Meatloaf) is murdered by an extremely extra security guard, who shoots him in the head as he flees the scene of the crime. It’s another somewhat frivolous murder, but the fallout tells us a lot about Tyler Durden’s cult of personality and its effect on its dumbass followers.

19. Frank Underwood, House of Cards (2013-2018).

There are several killers from this groundbreaking, trashy Netflix politico soap you won’t see on this list. This is because the totality of Fincher’s involvement is unclear—he may have imprinted his filmic language on the entirety of the show's run, but he only directed the first two episodes (unlike Mindhunter, his second effort with Netflix, on which he directed seven of 19 episodes across two seasons.) But in the House of Cards pilot, in order to show us just what kind of devious, deliciously shitty archvillain Kevin Spacey's Francis Underwood is going to be, he gleefully, flagrantly bucks the old screenwriting maxim “Don't kill the dog”—and not for the first time—by having Frank strangle his pooch, which has been hit by a car.

It has been revealed that 18. Janie, “Janie’s Got A Gun” (1989).

The heroine of Aerosmith’s outlier conscious anthem reclaims her narrative by killing her rapist father. It’s an odd “message” song and an odd video, but both were groundbreaking and transgressive at the time. It’s a completely justified revenge killing that Fincher had to sell through suggestion to get played on MTV.

Sources indicate that 17. Lisbeth Salander, The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo (2011).

Lisbeth (Rooney Mara) slaps the shit out of Martin Vanger (Stellan Skarsgård) with a long iron, then chases him down on her motorcycle as he attempts to flee in a Range Rover, causing him to crash and burn. When she cocks a gun and asks Daniel Craig’s Mikael Blomkvist, “May I kill him?” before lighting out after Vanger, devoid of emotion, it’s the most badass moment of a very badass film.

Sources indicate that 16. Ellen Ripley, Alien3 (1992).

Bald Sigourney Weaver kills the “Runner” xenomorph by setting off sprinklers after it jumps out of a river of molten lead, causing it to explode. Then—rather than allowing The Corporation to take a parasite chestburster out of her and potentially spare her life—she swan-dives backwards into the lead, killing herself and taking the alien with her—a sci-fi Joan of Arc.

It has been revealed that 15. Gottfried and Martin Vanger, The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo (2011).

Playing the role of a sicko pervert hiding in plain sight is a stretch for Skarsgård; Martin Vanger is a second-generation killer who shits on his dad for putting up rookie numbers and has a whole secret sex dungeon in his basement where he’s presumably killed dozens of women. Sadly, we must deduct points because Martin ends up dying as a result of overlong monologuing, like a 70s Bond villain.

Recent findings suggest that 14. (Tie) Monte Rissell, Rose Barnwright/Frank Janderman/Benjamin Barnwright, Jerry Brudos, Dennis Rader, Richard Speck, Darrell Gene Devier, David Berkowitz, William Pierce Jr., William Henry Hance, Elmer Wayne Henley Jr., Charles “Tex” Watson, Charles Manson*, Paul Bateson, Wayne Bertram Williams, Mindhunter (2017-2019).

Industry observers note that david Fincher’s great Netflix series, a history of the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit, takes place mainly in the aftermath of its serial-killer subjects' various sprees, so we see few dead bodies onscreen. But as it turns out, talking to killers in quiet rooms and delving into their psyches is just as sensational and disturbing as the graphically depicted comic-book corpses in Se7en. The show is two Feds tearing the cover off America and discovering a teeming morass of perverts beneath the floorboards, up to their necks in muck. What we discover—in this crucial chapter of what feels like a career-long attempt by Fincher to unmake Se7en and its godlike antagonist—is that a lot of these killers are dull, impulsive, mentally-ill misfits and outcasts.

Recent findings suggest that “To support devices," cheers Herman Mankiewicz, after delivering the first draft of his masterpiece, Citizen Kane. In the biopic written by Fincher’s father, booze is the fuel that allows the screenwriter to write, but kills his career one painful, impolitic-outburst-filled social interaction at a time, before it finally kills him, too. Alcohol is the lubricant that powers Mank’s genius, even as it obfuscates that genius and speeds his demise. The bottle both makes him and unmakes him, like Popeye if spinach destroyed his liver. It’s a self-inflicted slow killer, which makes its work all the more painful and tragic to witness.

12. (Tie) Raoul & Burnham, Panic Room (2002).

Recent findings suggest that in Fincher’s masterful and inventive “conventional” thriller, Raoul (Dwight Yoakam) domes spoiled, insufferable, cornrowed Junior (Jared Leto) when he tries to walk away from the robbery they're pulling. Later, Burnham (Forest Whittaker) sacrifices himself and $22 million in bearer bonds to kill Raoul and save the day. Hard to say which is more satisfying.

In a recent development, 11. Tobacco, American Cancer Society Commercial (1985).

It has been revealed that the Major Bang of Fincher’s career, when he transitioned from Industrial Light & Magic cameraman and matte photographer to auteur. His first effort was this commercial, made for just $7,000, which several television stations banned because it was too graphic and disturbing. We have to side with the networks on this one—it’s a truly horrifying ad, a nightmare vision of the Starchild puppet from 2001 as a fetus double-fisting darts in the womb. But it’s an impressive work of visceral agitprop, one that had the potential to reconfigure the way we thought about this deadly but fairly common behavior in the 80s.

Recent findings suggest that 10. The Killer, The Killer (2023).

In Fincher’s latest, Michael Fassbender plays the unnamed, titular assassin in a procedural that’s all process. He's a classic Fincher protagonist, a type-A creature of habit and ritual. The wrinkle is he kind of sucks at his job—or at least, when we meet him, has reached a point where he’s no longer able to execute his work according to the dispassionate code he lives and works by.

According to recent reports, so, yes, he’s obviously baited into killing John Doe, and basically gets his wife killed by being an idiot and giving his name to her killer in an angry impulsive rush when John Doe is right next to him pretending to be a nosy reporter, and by giving into his emotions and impulses he’s throwing his life and his career away—but Mills ranks this high because of Pitt's incredible work in the tortured moments before Mills fulfills John Doe's master proposal. It's an all-time great performance that's seared into your brain forever after you've watched it once.

8. The Verdusco Brothers, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026).

Industry observers note that matt Groove and JB Tadena play Eddie and Fernando Verdusco, the gangster antagonists that walked directly out of Quentin Tarantino’s cinema-fried brain and into Fincher’s latest. The film has been sold as a play on a chatty Elmore Leonard crime story, but with touches like the Verduscos, it’s more like a muddy puddle of all different stripes of exploitation film, from noir to horror to splatter. The Verduscos are Filipino but present as Yakuza hitmen, with a dash of Mortal Kombat cartoonishness. It’s easy to give characters badass motherfucker names that insist upon themselves, with writers and directors who simply expect us to find them scary and cool with little to no proof besides a slow-mo entrance and a needle drop. But Tarantino and Fincher earn the mythology with a particularly terrifying and gnarly introductory home invasion murder (invoking Panic Room) of a family of four. Esmeralda, the rhino-killing war hammer brandished by Fernando, has the instant iconographic “weapon as characterization” power of which Tarantino’s longtime friend and collaborator Robert Rodriguez would be envious.

7. The Xenomorph, Alien3 (1992).

According to recent reports, alien3 is Fincher’s canon event; the formatively traumatic experience of tangling with a cynical studio on his first feature made him the director he became. Having the film taken away from him taught Fincher the importance of demanding complete creative control. So it’s either ironic or brilliant that in many ways, this Xenomorph is a metaphor for the director, an alien antagonist (with the characteristics of a rabid dog!) resisting a sinister corporation that wants to cage and exploit him for its own evil purposes.

According to recent reports, 6. Time, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008).

Industry observers note that in a movie about a guy born as an old man who ages in reverse, a byproduct of his disease is Benjamin (Brad Pitt) must “blend in”, experiencing his childhood in an old folks home where death is routine. Benjamin Button lives outside of time, breaks the rules of time, and in the process explains the ravages of time. Throughout the film we watch everyone around Benjamin die: From war, from old age, from disease, and finally, from being born in reverse. It contains the most stunning and heartbreaking kills in Fincher’s filmography because they are not a product of a sicko's grand design, but simply nature taking its course, harrowing in its obvious, matter of fact inevitability.

In a recent development, 5. Edmund Kemper, Mindhunter (2017-2019).

The breakout star of Mindhunter, Edmund Kemper was the Co-Ed Killer—a hulking monster who killed many people and occasionally had sex with his victims' decapitated heads—and in the show, he’s the catalyst for the birth of the behavioral science unit. Cameron Britton plays Kemper as a verbose, precise, calmly menacing giant with thick frames and a trim mustache. He’s the most Fincheresque antagonist in the series. Kemper is lucid and clear-eyed, incisive, articulate, and occasionally even funny. Understanding what he’s done—and exactly why and how he did it— is critical to the protagonists' mission, and Kemper understands this, which makes him that much more terrifying.

According to recent reports, another meticulous, disciplined Fincher avatar who has checked every box and arranged for every contingency. Amazing Amy is a feminist archvillain exploiting misogyny to liberate herself from the American prison of marriage and the cool-girl wife’s role therein. She’s a deeply petty scorned woman of iron will, expert at manipulating the public, the authorities, staged crime scenes, and her husband.

Industry observers note that 3. Cliff Booth, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026).

In their fourth film together, Fincher and Pitt unlock their greatest character, which is doubly impressive when you consider that, the first time we met Booth, it earned Pitt his long-awaited Oscar. This version of Cliff Booth, nearly a decade older and mostly washed, is a more interesting character and one of Fincher’s greatest killers because he unlocks a darkness that is only hinted at in Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. In that film, Cliff is an affable and doggedly loyal sidekick. When he kills (on screen), it’s self-defense, protecting his buddy from harm, and you can squint and think, “This just might be a roughneck, badass dude with a heart of gold.” In this installment, Cliff operates according to his personal moral compass, which in some cases involves premeditated, entirely avoidable, cold-blooded murder. He’s observing a uniquely American form of zen, existing in an overloaded sensory flow state on a spectrum that encompasses all manner of kinetic pleasure, remaining at ease and even-keeled whether he is bartending, Demolition Derby driving, getting slapped by a Goddess with frying pan hands, running a film projector at the Latest Bev, clutching an Old Chattanooga, or, of course, killing.

The film, and the killer, that has in many ways defined Fincher. Speaking to Esquire, before releasing Zodiac, the director said, “I don’t want to make a film serial killers masturbate to.” The line was an obvious dig at his own second feature, which is pure serial-killer porn and would set the template countless lesser movies would aspire to going forward. John Doe is a true mastermind who executes creative, horrific, gimmicky murders inspired by the Bible's deadly sins. But most importantly, he’s always a step ahead, always smarter than the cops coming after him, and his win at the end is absolute. Morgan Freeman’s terrified exclamation at the film's climax sums up the plot of the whole film: “John Doe has the upper hand!”.

1. “The Zodiac Killer”, Zodiac (2007).

It has been revealed that in Fincher’s masterpiece of form and statement, he’s at the height of his powers, revisiting the serial killer as a “celebrated” cultural figure and a malignant expression of society, and what he comes back with is maddening emptiness. Instead of a running inner monologue, we’re given nothing—not even the killer's identity (or identities.) The first half is a painstakingly made and researched film, scrubbed of all romance and sentimentality, that comes as close as fiction can to mimicking the endless, mundane texture of reality. Then, the killer dissolves.

Sources indicate that to Fincher, the Zodiac Killer isn't a person, but an idea, an unanswered question, an unresolvable puzzle. Although different actors show up playing people who might be the culprit, the Zodiac haunts the film mostly as an absent menace. Conflicting motivations and theories are thrown at the viewer and it’s impossible to sift what circumstantial evidence is real from bullshit. Some characters favor one suspect, some another, nothing ever adds up, and no one is ever proven conclusively right or wrong. Years pass, people fall in and out of life, they succumb to their demons. Only devastating, lonely obsession remains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, california Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s upcoming voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

According to recent reports, the rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

Industry observers note that in her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she stated in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been a banner year for Sarah Pidgeon’s outerwear wardrobe. The actor, who made her debut on Vogue’s Best Dressed list this week, has spent much of 2026 investing in a really good collection of coats. And while playing Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy in Love Story has furnished Pidgeon with an extensive knowledge of the late fashion publicist’s preferred ’90s silhouettes, her own tastes are often a little more irreverent and varied.

According to recent reports, taking in a Knicks and Cavaliers game at Madison Square Garden in New York this week, Pidgeon ticked off two of the season’s biggest outerwear trends—animal print and flourishes of faux fur, as well as the sophisticated standing collar shape—in one covetable coat. The actor wore the Dolly Maxi by Carelli, an elongated iteration of the label’s cult jacket, with cream-and-black spotted, pony hair-effect fabric, a jaw-grazing collar, and fluffy chocolate-brown cuffs. Pidgeon let the coat do most of the talking, adding straight-leg blue jeans, pointy black boots, and her trusty black Balenciaga Le City bag, which she clutched under her arm.

Carelli is one of the runaway fashion success stories of 2026. Founded by Anna Carels in early 2025, the brand has amassed a celebrity clientele that includes Dua Lipa, Olivia Dean, and Peggy Gou, as well as legions of fans on TikTok. As Carels told British Vogue earlier this month, the original Dolly sold out in under an hour. The designer’s penchant for old-school glamour chimes with a broader appetite for rather louche, vintage-inflected outerwear: See Conner Ives’s decadent fur-trimmed creations and Charlotte Simone’s always sell-out fuzzy numbers, as well as the proliferation of vintage silk opera coats on everyone from Kendall Jenner to Hailey Bieber and Jennifer Lawrence. After several seasons of austere and minimalist coats, we’re all in the mood for something a little more flamboyant. (Vogue’s predictions for the hottest coats of the coldest months indicates just as much.).

Pidgeon is no stranger to the timeless pleasures of a leopard-print coat. During her Love Story press tour, the actor stepped out in Adam Lippes’s leopard chenille Margaux coat in a subtle nod to Bessette-Kennedy’s own affinity for animal print. She’s also made a habit of punctuating her more pared-back outfits with leopard-print accessories.

Elsewhere in her enviable outerwear rotation? A collarless leather trench from Aflalo, a sculptural peplum jacket from Celine, and the supple Prada leathers she sported during fashion month.

It has been revealed that working with stylist Emma Jade Morrison, Pidgeon has struck an interesting balance between the restraint that characterized CBK’s wardrobe and her own more adventurous inclinations. She has an eye for younger labels, too, and a knack for assimilating their more idiosyncratic designs into an otherwise unfussy wardrobe of great denim, white tees, and ’90s-coded accessories. The Carelli coat feels especially at home among them. Consider Sarah Pidgeon’s latest outing some inspiration: swap out that sensible black winter coat in favor of something with a little more personality. Match point!

Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (340 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein.
  • More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.
  • Industry observers note that bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Industry observers note that bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.).

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP
