📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie.
  • Sources indicate that if you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly confirms they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening.
  • Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie. But there’s another tradition that's becoming increasingly popular.

Sources indicate that if you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly confirms they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening. The so-called “cousin walk,” when relatives sneak away to smoke weed, has become such a recognizable holiday ritual that it's now inspiring TikTok videos, memes, and an entire shopping event.

Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.

Green Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving, and it has become one of the year’s biggest shopping days for cannabis retailers. This year, it falls on November 25.

The term has been around since at least 2016, when cannabis delivery firm Eaze began using it after noticing a surge in purchases ahead of Thanksgiving.

According to MJBizDaily, cannabis retailers recorded approximately $138.5 million in sales on Green Wednesday in 2025, up from $132.4 million the previous year, based on data from cannabis market intelligence manufacturer BDSA.

While Green Wednesday is often described as the industry’s second-biggest shopping day behind 4/20, some retailers are seeing even stronger results.

According to recent reports, according to data RISE Dispensaries shared with Delish, Green Wednesday was its biggest sales day of 2025 and outperformed the notorious cannabis holiday 4/20. The manufacturer’s sales were roughly double an average Wednesday, while pre-rolls saw their strongest sales day of the year.

A major part of Green Wednesday’s cultural appeal comes from the infamous cousin walk—the tradition has become a recurring joke across social media, with TikTok users sharing videos about coordinating their annual walkabout. And, of course, brands are getting involved, too.

As Morning Brew reported, Jif referenced cousin walks in an Instagram promotion last year, while a Taco Bell and Hidden Valley collaboration played on a similar holiday joke. Cannabis brand Dogwalkers is also leaning into the tradition with a Cousin Walk Kit tied to Thanksgiving.

And while Green Wednesday and the cousin walk go hand in hand, cannabis use isn't limited to just the cousins.

A 2026 study from UC San Diego found that approximately 8.9% of Americans ages 65 and older had used cannabis in the previous year. Among those owners, 40.5% reported consuming cannabis through food or drinks. Meanwhile, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that 22.4% of American adults used cannabis in 2025.

Americans’ drinking habits are changing, too. A 2026 Gallup survey found that just 54% of U.S. adults consume alcohol, down from 62% in 2023. While the figures don't establish that people are replacing alcohol with cannabis, they reflect changing consumption habits. It seems people are increasingly opting out of Blackout Wednesday and opting into Green Wednesday.

The growing conversation around edibles also comes with an notable reminder: Cannabis-infused foods and drinks can take longer to produce noticeable effects than inhaled cannabis, and they should always be clearly labeled and kept away from children.

Between the sales numbers, viral cousin-walk jokes, and brands embracing the tradition, Green Wednesday is becoming a recognizable part of the Thanksgiving season. So when someone inevitably asks whether anyone wants to go for a walk after dinner, just know that an entire industry has been preparing for that moment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a upcoming personality. Unlike plain noodles, which rapidly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Industry observers note that season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Sources indicate that heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Recent findings suggest that melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Recent findings suggest that scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Santiago Lastra Wants You to Stop Overthinking Mexican Food

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Santiago Lastra might have become a mathematician if it weren’t for a box of Ritz crackers.
  • Recent findings suggest that then, at 15, Lastra spotted a crab dip recipe on the back of a cracker box.
  • Recent findings suggest that the chef has spent the past month touring the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Santiago Lastra might have become a mathematician if it weren’t for a box of Ritz crackers. Growing up in Cuernavaca, Mexico, the future chef behind London restaurants KOL and Fonda was the sort of kid with more of an appetite for national math competitions. “There would be four questions and five hours to answer those four questions,” he remembers. “I loved that. I wanted to do that for the rest of my life.”.

Recent findings suggest that then, at 15, Lastra spotted a crab dip recipe on the back of a cracker box. He made it for his family and watched as an ordinary day changed shape around something he had cooked. “I became obsessed with the idea that you can create a special occasion just by cooking something for someone,” he says. The mathematical brain moved into the kitchen. In his first cookbook, Mexican Soul: A New Style of Cooking, Lastra writes about the magic of both disciplines: starting with a few ingredients (or figures) and a recipe (or equation) and creating something greater than the sum of its parts.

Recent findings suggest that the chef has spent the past month touring the U.S. in support of the book: He’s made tacos at New York’s Santo Taco, cooked at Yucatan-style seafood spot Holbox in Los Angeles, and enlisted The Bear’s Will Poulter to put a Mexican spin on the Italian beef sandwich at Chicago’s storied Mr. Beef (the real-life inspiration for the show’s original restaurant). Along the way, he’s helped introduce American audiences to a philosophy of Mexican cooking that is as resourceful and intuitive as it is traditional and communal.

According to recent reports, it’s an instinct that has taken Lastra on a circuitous journey back home. He started out cooking Italian food, then left Mexico for kitchens in Spain. Various fascinations with French techniques, the experimentalism of Mugaritz, and Latest Nordic cuisine followed. “As a young kid, when you leave Mexico, you feel that you made it,” he says. “It took me a long time to realize that what we had in Mexico was really the answer.” Lastra began applying Mexican techniques to local ingredients in Scandinavia, then traveled and cooked across 27 countries. Returning to Mexico to work on Noma’s Tulum pop-up allowed him to look at his homeland with newly curious eyes. “Being Mexican became my superpower,” he says. “I was able to share culture through food, and it opened the doors to the world for me.”.

It has been revealed that KOL was his attempt to make that realization tangible: the Marylebone restaurant that Lastra opened in 2020 cooks Mexican food through seasonal British ingredients. Fonda, its more casual and rambunctious sibling, followed four years later. “I wanted KOL to be one of the best restaurants in the world,” he says, to prove “that Mexican food should be recognized at the level of all the best cuisines in the world.” Not everyone Lastra hoped to touch could ever make it to his London spots or the global pop-ups. “What really makes a difference culturally is the food that people do at home,” he says. “Home cooking is more personal.”.

Sources indicate that mexican Soul posed some questions. How do you cook food that feels fundamentally Mexican without fresh masa, the right dried chillies, or a specialist grocer? Lastra didn’t want readers buying a two-pound bag of chipotle for one dinner. “I had to change the way I think,” he notes. He began writing upcoming rules for the weeknight home cook, rather than an ingredients-led chef. The transition required its own education. He pored over British supermarket aisles, and during a family beach vacation, Lastra locked himself inside to watch hours of Jamie Oliver. He and his brother Eduardo, his collaborator on the book and at KOL, went into a supermarket and decreed that nothing for the shoot could be ordered elsewhere.

“It tasted great,” he recalls. “I was like, wow… I think I’ve been overcomplicating myself all my life.” Just like in his childhood math competitions, limitations could provide the route to a more interesting solution. The book’s first half teaches some culinary grammar: Sourness, heat, sweetness, smoke, fat, and masa are defined and built into pillar dishes such as guacamole and quesadillas to demonstrate how those sensations work together. “Every time I create a dish, I always see flavors,” Lastra explains. “They’re like your paintings, your colors.”.

According to recent reports, the second half gets freer: tomato and cherry aguachile, potato rajas tamales, asparagus pipián. Innovating beyond traditional Mexican cooking, this style is rooted in the cuisine’s history and designed to work with seasonal, local, and accessible ingredients from wherever its cook lives. Lastra resists the idea of Mexican food as something stuck in amber. “The most beautiful thing about Mexican cooking, or Mexican food and Mexican culture in general, is that it keeps evolving,” he says. His proudest—and most last-minute addition—was a tortilla. Nearly defeated by the challenge of creating one without corn masa, Lastra had the novel idea of using mashed potato. Combining it with potato starch, he pressed and cooked the dough, and after days of tweaking, “suddenly it worked and it puffed!” It made it into the book just before printing.

Home-testing in the Lastra household has been even sweeter. After we speak, Lastra’s mother—who almost never cooks—is making the book’s mackerel a la Veracruzana for her sons. She’s already sending photographs as she shops for ingredients. “I think she’s never cooked a specific recipe from a cookbook in her life,” he says. “So that’s going to be such a highlight.”.

Below, Santiago Lastra’s recipe for albóndigas and Mexican rice, two ways.

Meatballs came to Mexico from the Middle East during the colonial period. They’re a classic of central Mexican home cooking, and are also served in casual eateries called fondas, where they are served with rice and bread or tortillas. The sauces they are served with vary from loose sauces made with cooked green tomatillos to rich tomato and guajillo chilli-based broths. I serve mine in a tomato caldillo with Mexican rice—a classic from our hometown. This is one of my favorite Mexican dishes, and one I would often choose to make if I am hosting friends for dinner.

Red rice is present at most lunches for any Mexican growing up, whether at home or eaten in a fonda. The preparation is simple: rice with peas and carrots, cooked in a tomato and chilli caldillo. The result is a spicy, umami rice with a beautiful color. Serve with stews and tortillas.

In a recent development, like the red version, this preparation adds a bit of spice, texture, and umami to plain rice. It’s served with all sorts of stews and other dishes in central Mexico, and also with broths like chicken consomé—the kind your mom might make for you when you’re unwell. Fresh jalapeños add a beautiful spicy finish. Perfect with chicken or any other proteins and refried beans.

Mexican Soul, Santiago Lastra (Quadrille) is out now.

Independents decide the election, again!

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E.
  • In a recent development, once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep.
  • “We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

In a recent development, independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also demonstrates that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

It has been revealed that despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

Recent findings suggest that in the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top concern concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent mentioned it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent stated his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Sources indicate that neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls highlighted that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Recent findings suggest that independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

Sources indicate that at a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent remarked the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Industry observers note that democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

Recent findings suggest that david Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy concerns, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

In a recent development, if you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

The Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

It has been revealed that mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

In a recent development, according to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up newly introduced recipes.

It has been revealed that since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

According to recent reports, note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a latest pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

According to recent reports, to a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#170479. The Best Cold-Weather Cocktails to Drink This Holiday Season

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2052 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Cold-Weather Cocktails to Drink This Holiday Season

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I typically take a less-is-more approach when it comes to my beverage choices.
  • A spirited sip that summons the mood of a crackling fireplace and the flavors of a Christmas kitchen.
  • There are many paths a cold-weather cocktail may take.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I typically take a less-is-more approach when it comes to my beverage choices. Having been burned one too many times by the flavor-packed ‘ingenuity’ of a bar’s signature cocktail, I’ve come to the conclusion that a martini, Negroni, or gin and tonic are better suited to my spartan palate. But once the holidays roll around, well, my fidelity to simplicity goes out the window, and I am an enthusiastic proprietor of the cozy cocktail.

What’s a cozy cocktail? Exactly what you think it is. A spirited sip that summons the mood of a crackling fireplace and the flavors of a Christmas kitchen. That transports you to a snowed-in cabin in Lapland, or a bustling holiday market in Germany. And I’m not talking about kitschy cocktails afflicted by crushed-up candy canes and artificial syrups—no, no. These are recipes that chase the outer limits of mixology, bringing together all that is merry and bright and elegantly transmuting it into your glass.

There are many paths a cold-weather cocktail may take. Traditional classics, like eggnog and hot toddies, are always welcome. For something theatrical, a smoked tipple does the trick (top marks for those performed tableside). For an off-the-charts cozy cocktail, those infused with seasonal spices will leave you deliriously jolly. And if you can’t bear to part ways with your old fashioned or espresso martini, take solace in knowing there are ways to ‘winter-fy’ these quintessential favorites.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re ready to raise a glass of something cozy in the coming weeks, let the guide below inform your order. And for those who wish to whip up cocktails for a festive fête at home, don’t miss the recipes at the end. Bar carts at the ready!

According to recent reports, the holidays present a decadent array of creamy cocktails calibrated specifically for the season. Take eggnog, for example. This rich tipple originated from a hot, milky, ale-adjacent drink called ‘posset’ that was enjoyed during Britain’s medieval era. Somewhere along the timeline, eggs joined the party, and several hundred years later, we’ve arrived at our modern-day recipes that consist of milk, heavy whipping cream, sugar, eggs, and nutmeg (spiked with rum, bourbon, or brandy). A boozy holiday milkshake, if you like.

Recent findings suggest that over at Smithereens in the East Village, head bartender Jacob Dorman wanted to make an eggnog with their in-house label rum, but decided to do an egg flip variation to show the versatility of the rum. (For reference, the main difference between an egg flip and eggnog is that a traditional flip leaves the dairy out.) “People always think of rum as a tropical spirit, but it can be warming and comforting too,” Dorman says. He uses a squash amaro for his flip, which “is like drinking pumpkin pie (in a good way).”.

Another creamy drink that foregoes the use of eggs is coquito. This Puerto Rican holiday cocktail typically uses coconut milk, cream of coconut, evaporated milk, sweetened condensed milk, vanilla extract, cinnamon, and ground nutmeg—spiked with rum. In a similar spirit, at The Wig Shop in Boston, beverage director Oscar Simoza is at the moment serving up a Venezuelan-inspired take on eggnog. It’s made with banana peel-infused rum, batido de cambur (ripe banana and milk), and arequipe (caramelized milk). Notes of anise and cinnamon, alongside a hint of amaro, come together for a cocktail that is sublimely silky.

The Brandy Alexander is another perennial classic. It’s made with brandy or cognac, dark crème de cacao, heavy cream, and freshly grated nutmeg for garnish. One of my favorite variations is at Bar Rêve in Cobble Hill. “Ours is an après-ski homage,” co-founder Victor Triebel claims. They pair a base of cognac with a layer of Frangelico whipped cream, finished with freshly grated nutmeg. “There’s nothing more luxurious than a warming brandy cocktail to end the evening,” Triebel adds.

During the chilliest months of the year, a cocktail encircled by fragrant smoke is just what the doctor ordered. Last winter, I found myself in the grand lobby of the Carlton Hotel St. Moritz, where drinks are served beside a stone fireplace and arrive via trolley cart. Their Piz Nair Mule—presented in a glass case—is inspired by a mountain that rises 3,057 meters above the Engadin Valley. Once the case is opened, a gentle cloud of smoke escapes, revealing the cocktail and miniature alpine landscape, complete with a moss-covered mountain and tiny mountaineers traversing the summit. The cocktail itself is a soothing blend of fresh thyme and rosemary, spicy ginger, and lime.

It has been revealed that if you can’t make it all the way to Switzerland this year, fret not, because San Ysidro Ranch in Montecito, California, has an entire menu dedicated to its tableside smoked cocktails. I’ve had the Smoking Pig Poke, which combines rye whiskey, averna, Luxardo maraschino, and a bacon-wrapped brandied cherry—all smoked with cherry wood. (They also serve cocktails smoked with oak, hickory, pecan, and pear woods—in case you’re picky about such things.) And if you’d like to impress your friends and try your hand at your own smoked cocktails, this smoke infuser would make an excellent holiday gift.

In a recent development, distilling the holiday season’s rich baking spices into a cocktail is nothing short of alchemy. Cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, cardamom, allspice—each offers its own shade of warmth, and can be used as liquor infusions, spiced syrups, bitters, or simply garnishes.

Recent findings suggest that at the newly opened Thai restaurant, Hommali, head bartender Patrick Cura created their Horchata Oolong cocktail, blending tequila, shochu, and sweet vermouth that’s been infused with oolong and umami bitters. “We torch a cinnamon stick over the glass for the garnish so you get an initial hit of baking spice at the first sip,” he shares. “It feels like a warm hug in a glass, which is particularly enjoyable when the temps start to drop.”.

Sources indicate that over at The Portrait Bar inside The Fifth Avenue Hotel, bar director Darryl Chan’s Marrakesh cocktail is inspired by the spice markets of Morocco. And further downtown at abcV in the Flatiron District, the Saffron Mylk rum cocktail is a blend of spices and saffron, heated with oat milk and honey, then finished with lashings of nutmeg. “The aroma from the nutmeg gives a wonderful warmth, with the heady spice evoking the holidays,” Chris Moore, director of beverage at Jean-Georges Restaurants, notes.

And if you’re searching for something a bit lighter, head for Williamsburg dive Shenanigans for their spiced vodka cran, featuring vodka, mulled wine with baking spices, lemon, and soda. (Starting December 2, Shenanigans will kick off their holiday pop-up serving festive cocktails through the new year—make haste.).

While the holidays have spurred legendary cocktail creations aplenty, if you prefer to stick to what you know, look for seasonal riffs on the classics. Hot cocoa is a wonderful place to start. You can spike your beloved hot chocolate with everything from aged rum and bourbon to cointreau and Bailey’s Irish cream. At Limo Bar in the East Village, their Santa’s Coffee cocktail dials up the cozy by pairing Irish whiskey and coffee with maple syrup and salted maple cream.

On a recent visit to the newly opened Bar CC, I ordered the Vesuvio, which is their spin on a coffee Boulevardier. The cocktail layers coffee-infused bourbon with cacao, tonic bean, amontillado sherry, Barolo Chinato, Campari, and Cappelletti rosso. The cocktail is then clarified with heated milk that’s been enriched with mascarpone. (Professional mixology here; do not attempt at home.) But wait! I haven’t even arrived at the best part: an edible lace doily is delicately draped over the glass, resulting in the most elegant riff on a Boulevardier you or I have ever encountered.

For the espresso martini devout among us, head for Pinky Swear to order the Cloud 9, which is an espresso martini garnished with a torched marshmallow. Or if you’re an old fashioned fanatic, take note of the Outtake at Upcoming Orleans’s Cure bar, which is seasoned with warm walnut and crisp ginger. Even clear spirits can receive the holiday treatment—at Dandelion in the West Village, their Poire None cocktail swirls together tequila, mezcal, ginger, allspice, yellow Chartreuse, and pear cider for an autumnal riff on the timeless mule. And at Dean’s, rather than relying on brandy or whiskey to conjure the cozies, their winter-friendly take on a classic sbagliato features sloe gin and elderflower liqueur for a deeper, fruitier character.

When in doubt, if you have a go-to cocktail but want to get into the spirit of the season, ask your bartender what they’ve got up their sleeve.

It has been revealed that not drinking alcohol? There are plenty of cozy mocktails that still fit the prompt. Beverages like eggnog, coquito, hot toddies, and hot chocolate can all be created with as much depth and complexity as their boozy counterparts—just skip the liquor part at the end. The Pear of Aces at Golden Steer is an aromatic hot toddy that simmers whole cloves, cinnamon, and star anise with lush pear nectar and melted lemon sherbet.

Recent findings suggest that or there’s the spirit-free amaretto sour at The Lobby Bar inside Hotel Chelsea, which doubles down on roasted flavors. This cocktail uses a zero-proof Amaretto liqueur made of roasted almonds from Puglia, plus a roasted green tea that’s acidified with lemon juice. “The cocktail is served up with a floater of honey-miso whipped cream, to replicate the head of egg white foam from a traditional sour-style cocktail,” shares Brian Evans, the director of bars at Sunday Hospitality.

Throwing a holiday party and need a few cozy cocktail ideas? Continue below for libations that will get everyone into the spirit of the season.

Directions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker and shake hard. Double strain into a coupe and garnish with grated chocolate.

“The Grasshopper is usually credited to Tujague's in Latest Orleans. It's a simple drink: crème de menthe, crème de cacao, and a splash of Franca menta and fresh cream, shaken until frothy and served a cool, pale green. Mint and chocolate taste like candy canes and peppermint bark, and the cream makes it smooth and soft. The green looks right at home by a tree or under twinkling lights. It's light and festive, a little nostalgic, and closer to dessert in a glass than to a cocktail” - Linden Pride, principal, Dante Elizabeth Street.

Recent findings suggest that directions: Run the apples through an extractor to separate the juice from the solids, letting the juice pour directly into a frothing pitcher. Add the sauce and bourbon. Steam all ingredients with a steam wand as though preparing milk for a latte. Pour into a heated mug.

Toddy Sauce Directions: Toast eight cinnamon sticks and four grams of whole black pepper in a pot. Add 650 grams Lambic (Duchess de Bourgogne), 650 grams Maple syrup, 12 grams turmeric and nine grams black pepper. Bring to a quick boil then lower to a simmer for 10 minutes. Cool and strain into a deli.

In a recent development, “Fresh pressed green apples are some of my favorite things to work with because the texture is so frothy coming out of the Breville. Steaming them doubles down on the intensity of the technique. The spice blend of turmeric, black pepper, and cinnamon evokes strong winter memories without falling into ‘pumpkin spice’ or Angostura bitters. Everything remains both familiar and impossibly fresh.” - Owen Gibler, Beverage Director, Bar Roza.

Directions: Beat egg yolks and sugars until lightened in color and texture. In a separate bowl, combine dairy, spirits, salt, and nutmeg. Slowly stream the mixture into the beaten egg yolks and sugar while mixing. Once homogeneous, transfer to a sterile glass container and refrigerate for at least one week, ideally one month. Serve with freshly grated nutmeg.

“An elevated take on the holiday classic, Beckon’s Aged Eggnog is prepared months in advance, allowing bonded bourbon, Armagnac, aged and white rum to mellow alongside egg yolks, cream, milk, sugar and nutmeg. Aged for at least one week (though a month is even better), the high-proof spirits develop an almost cheesecake-like tang, resulting in a rich, warming cocktail finished simply with freshly grated nutmeg.” - Joseph Buckley, beverage director, Paired Hospitality.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving asks a lot of us (and our ovens!). From making the turkey to all of the casseroles and sides, don’t even get me started on dessert. You’ve got a lot on your plate, so we’re trying to make the massive turkey day a little easier. Appetizers are my favorite part of the meal: little bites that pack so much flavor and fun into the start of the big feast, so you’ve gotta make them count. We’ve got some clever, simple shortcuts to help you whip up appetizers that will impress your guests without adding to your stress.

Whether you’re looking for quick and easy last-minute options or want something more elaborate, we’ve got something on this list for you. Need more Thanksgiving hosting ideas? Check out our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes and Thanksgiving cocktails!

Pumpkin Spice Hot Honey Brie Bites.

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

In a recent development, there is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. These would be a fun alternative to biscuits or Parker House rolls at Thanksgiving or another big family meal.

It has been revealed that having multiple Thanksgivings this year? Want to transform your leftovers from one into something incredible for the next? Look no further than this stuffed bread ring—it's gorgeous and super easy, thanks to store-bought crescent roll dough.

With all of the elements of stuffing plus the added flaky and butter benefits of biscuits, this pull-apart stuffing bread just might start a tug-of-war situation at your table when you grab for a slice.

Industry observers note that it’s a tail as old as time: It’s right before Thanksgiving dinner, and your guests don’t want a full meal but are feeling a little peckish. Try a bird of a different feather this year, and serve this festive and impressive fruit and cheese display as the centerpiece of your holiday app table.

It has been revealed that these Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. Preparing these potato skins is simple; all you need for this recipe are Thanksgiving leftovers and a few additional pantry staples: potatoes and cheddar cheese.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to find a party appetizer that’s more beloved than a cheese log—or its alternate form, the cheese ball. Here, dried sweetened cranberries, walnuts, and fresh thyme conjure a holiday feeling, while a little honey complements the sweet-tart fruit.

These are a fan favorite every fall. They always disappear within minutes, probably because the combo of salty, creamy brie, sweet-tart cranberry sauce, and crunchy pecans is PERFECT.

In a recent development, fall desserts may get all the attention once autumn comes around, but I'm here to say that seasonal appetizers deserve their share of the spotlight—especially these adorable pizza-stuffed pumpkins. Stuffed with creamy ricotta, these biscuit-based bites are baked to golden perfection before being brushed with a flavor-packed garlic butter.

It has been revealed that just like our famous cranberry brie bites, these little guys are hard to put down! They're the perfect amount of sweet and savory, so you can serve them before or after the massive meal.

Sausage Stuffing Bites With Cranberry Sauce.

According to recent reports, stuffing, inside the turkey or out, is a Thanksgiving staple. The only thing better? MORE. STUFFING. Enter this bite-sized, stuffing-centered appetizer with a tangy, three-ingredient dipping sauce (just cranberry sauce, honey, and Dijon).

Industry observers note that even if you're not serving turkey this Thanksgiving doesn't mean you can't get in on the theme. Enter: this adorable cheeseball. We used carrots, pecans, pretzels, and bell peppers to create the iconic look, but feel free to substitute them with different ingredients for what you have on hand. Serve it with crackers and use the decorations as dippers too!

These sweet potato bites have a crunchy, herbaceous crust, with a sweet, silky inside that, when topped with a light drizzle of honey, will have you craving them again and again. Once you bite through the crust, the sweet potato mixes with that melted, nutty Gruyère for a dream flavor combination that works SO well.

Cranberry Brie Jalapeño Poppers.

Cranberry brie bites are by far one of our favorite appetizers for the holidays, but jalapeño poppers also have place in our hearts too... So why not combine them? The spice of the jalapeño goes so well with the tart cranberries.

To make these, we stuff baby bella mushrooms with garlicky, herby breadcrumbs and plenty of cheese. Stuff them ahead of time and bake them off when you're ready for the most Thanksgiving-friendly appetizer ever.

Cranberry Brie Pull-Apart Bread.

Pull-apart bread reaches a whole new level, thanks to brie and cranberry sauce. Use your favorite homemade sauce recipes, but store-bought works too if you're short for time.

Caramelized Onion & Goat Cheese Bites.

Industry observers note that little puff pastry squares get topped with caramelized onions and a little crumbled goat cheese for an easy appetizer that always wows. The final step is a light drizzle of honey for that salty sweet combination everyone will love.

Sources indicate that if you’re a fan of our cranberry brie bites, we’ve got news for you: There’s a newly introduced app in town, and it’s inspired by another fan fave, baked feta pasta. These features the flavors you know and love, all nestled into bite-sized cups of golden crescent roll dough.

There's something very classic about the crescent roll dough flavor, so we tend to gravitate toward it, but puff pastry or even biscuit dough should both work here, too.

Think this sounds like a strange combo? You've gotta trust us on this one. If the aroma of toasted puff pastry, roasted apples, and nutty cheddar cheese doesn’t wake up your spirit… we're not sure what will.

Sources indicate that rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to concern subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

According to recent reports, the letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia mentioned. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”.

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

Recent findings suggest that he also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

It has been revealed that and Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and Newly introduced York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Sources indicate that garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability challenges, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin stated.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

According to recent reports, every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

In a recent development, to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

It has been revealed that drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

According to recent reports, to a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Industry observers note that place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Name a better feeling than this: you’ve got a plate of picky bits piled high, a glass of fizz in hand, a fire on, your phone Bricked, and a film you’ve seen one hundred times lined up. Winter gets a bad rap, for many reasons, but this Christmas scene? A true flow state.

For some reason, Christmas is the only time of year when we’re not just willing to watch films we could recite by heart while half-asleep—it seems to be a centerpiece of the holiday.

Recent findings suggest that for many of us, those comfort watches simply have to be Christmas rom-coms (perhaps with a bit of Home Alone thrown in). There’s an unrivaled comfort to a love story that plays out to a stripped-back piano version of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas,” some fake snow, and a will-they-won’t-they Latest Year’s countdown. Maybe it’s the champs talking, but you truly can’t beat it.

To that end, here are some of the best Christmas rom-coms of all time.

Recent findings suggest that based on the newspaper column and subsequent book by Helen Fielding, the story is told through diary entries by the titular Bridget Jones, played by Renée Zellweger (as you probably well know). Of course, Bridget is the blueprint for the frazzled Englishwoman trope—with her laddered tights, cooking mishaps, and pretty much always saying and doing slightly the wrong thing—but who could fail to fall for her? Certainly not Daniel Cleaver (Hugh Grant) or Mark Darcy (Colin Firth), whose rivalry culminates in one of the greatest slapstick brawls in cinematic history. So genuinely funny, heartwarming, and perfectly cast, we can even begrudgingly overlook the problematic fact that Bridget’s weight was a subplot of its own.

Starring Will Ferrell as an enormous yet child-like elf who was born human but grew up in the North Pole with Santa and his crew, this John Favreau-directed film became an instant classic upon release in 2003. With anyone else but Ferrell in the lead, this movie could have flopped, but he plays Buddy to perfection. (Hands up if you still quote, “Daddy, Daddy, I’m in love and I don’t care who knows it!”) Buddy travels to Latest York to find his real father, played by James Caan, who turns out to be a grump who has absolutely zero festive cheer. Luckily, his son is an elf who can help him discover the true meaning of Christmas—and turn his failing children’s book manufacturer around in the process. The rom part of this rom-com is courtesy of Zooey Deschanel, who plays the department store worker who falls for Buddy.

Christmas doesn’t officially start until you’ve done your annual rewatch of Richard Curtis’s Love, Actually (we don’t make the rules!). The ultimate ensemble movie, with its various subplots culminates in a grande finale involving a school nativity play, this film is like seven little films in one. There’s Martine McCutcheon as Downing Street staffer Natalie; Hugh Grant as the prime minister we’d all like in real life; Colin Firth as the stern, broken-hearted one who flees to France; Liam Neeson as the widower; Keira Knightley and Chiwetel Ejiofor as the newlyweds and Andrew Lincoln as their borderline-creepy best pal; Bill Nighy as a washed-up rocker; and Laura Linney nabbing the hottest office co-worker to ever live. Emma Thompson, meanwhile, delivers one of the most devastating scenes you’ll ever see (Joni Mitchell CDs were never the same again). Also featured: an ideal soundtrack (Dido, Gabrielle, Texas) that your mom would have cleaned to in the Noughties.

Recent findings suggest that A highly-strung New Yorker, Meredith Morton, played by Sarah Jessica Parker, goes to Connecticut to meet her boyfriend Everett Stone’s bohemian, eccentric, and extremely close-knit family at their home for the holidays. Everett (Dermot Mulroney) looks to propose with a family heirloom (ahh! The family stone!), but after a rocky start, his family is going to need some persuading that Meredith is right for him…and them. It’s not your straightforward warm and fuzzy movie, but it’s far more unique than anything made today, and the cast really is stellar (the late Diane Keaton, Claire Danes, Rachel McAdams, and Luke Wilson all appear). One to rewatch before the sequel, The Families Stone (yes, really), drops in November 2027.

Nancy Meyers outdid herself with this one. The set-up is simple: Amanda (Cameron Diaz) and Iris (Kate Winslet) are suffering the most dreadful romantic woes thanks to the men in their lives, played by Edward Burns and Rufus Sewell. And so they find themselves on an early sort of Airbnb to initiate a house swap, with Amanda staying in Iris’s chocolate box Cotswolds home while Iris jets to Amanda’s Los Angeles mansion. They are on a mission to “find themselves” and, by golly, that involves some snogging. Iris falls for musician Miles, played by Jack Black, Amanda gets Graham, a widowed father-of-two played by Jude Law. It’s all so lovely, there’s rarely been a film more capable of calming one’s nervous system.

Industry observers note that not to be confused with Nancy Meyers’s bicontinental confection—nor with 2019’s Last Christmas, starring Emilia Clarke and Henry Golding and co-written by Emma Thompson—Last Holiday, directed by Wayne Wang (Joy Luck Club, Maid in Manhattan), is loosely based on a 1950 British film of the same name. This version stars Queen Latifah as Georgia Byrd, a selfless saleswoman from New Orleans who, upon learning she is terminally ill, books a lavish Christmastime visit to the Grandhotel Pupp in the Czech Republic, where she intends to squeeze every last indulgent moment out of the weeks she has left. If all that sounds a bit maudlin, trust that Queen Latifah makes an incredibly winning (and glamorous) leading lady, Timothy Hutton is delectable as a big-business villain, and LL Cool J is the love interest (!). (Yes, Gérard Depardieu is in there too, but don’t let him scare you off!).

I long for the weird days when Vince Vaughan starred in rom-coms. Sure, he’s a sort of unlikely leading man, but his ability to gruffly subvert a genre? No one does it like Vaughan. Four Christmases sees him star opposite fellow rom-com royalty Reese Witherspoon; they play Brad and Kate, a couple who avoid Christmas with their divorced parents each year by claiming to do charity work abroad (when they’re really going on a tropical holiday). One year, their flights get canceled because of widespread fog, their lie is outed by a news reporter on live TV, and they find themselves having to visit all four parents in a single day for four different Christmas celebrations.

  • A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Recent findings suggest that as Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie noted his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he stated, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The newly introduced bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

According to recent reports, now that the upcoming petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Recent findings suggest that other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Industry observers note that allies of the problem in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”.

It has been revealed that “Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie noted. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor.".

The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Recent findings suggest that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

It has been revealed that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

It has been revealed that transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

During the interregnum between the departure of Seán McGirr and the arrival of his as-yet-unnamed successor, McQueen is taking a look at itself. For this pre-fall collection, the studio team used its take on the house codes as a mirror, focusing upon each member’s individual specialisms while ensuring the whole ensemble remained coherently connected.

In both womenswear and menswear, the objective was sophistication stimulated by visceral twists and visual misdirection. The at-first-glance glossy croc leather of pants worn under a sky-blue jacket in womenswear, and as a matching black set in menswear, was denim treated with a raised pigment print. An asymmetric lapel and lighter internal construction relaxed the formality of a gray checked men’s suit worn over a frogged shirt. There was an echo of British countrywear in a subtly snake-patterned brown wool jacquard women’s suit whose integrated leather-strapped harness cinched just below the bust. A trailing-wrap, flat-fronted Prince of Wales check kilt, pleated behind, was rendered in an unexpectedly light fabrication. The full-skirted strapless dress that closed the lookbook was fashioned from a specially developed black lace lacquered to create a sheeny surface flash. Golden viscose suiting shimmered.

Industry observers note that in knitwear, the tangled skeins of spider lace—derived from Alexander McQueen’s 1994 Banshee collection—were reinterpreted in a fine openwork jacquard of cotton backed with silk. A closely fitted dress in shades of metallic jacquard was based on a laser-cut lace piece from the house’s spring 2012 collection and featured a grille of serrated-edged rib cage cutouts on the back.

The corsetry that informed some ready-to-wear was also reflected in the finely drawn lacing applied to boots and pumps. Sharply chiseled men’s formal shoes featured gently tarnished and spackled metal hardware. On some women’s pumps, additional spathes of almost patently glossy leather, worked with metal threads to allow their shape to be manipulated, were designed to resemble calla lilies. These also featured in embroidery or print; in pink against a graduated red ground on skirts and shirting, on the sleeves of a biker jacket, and through the blinds of a fitted dress in whose harness structure was slung with strips of sliced leather.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, going back to her early days on Latest York’s Hot 97, longtime radio host and veteran interviewer Angie Martinez has been getting rappers to drop their guard and engage in revealing, insightful conversations for over 30 years. Hot 97 was where you went to see Angie, Funkmaster Flex and the like if you had a new freestyle to get off, news to break, drama to address. But Martinez didn’t just get scoop; she facilitated dialogues that would often show some of the game’s most furtive rappers entirely at ease. Her show was a destination, her reporting was crucial, and her stature was reflected in a moniker: The Voice of New York.

In the years since, Angie has migrated to Power 105.1 while also moving into the podcast space. But there was always one piece of lore that loomed over her career: she was sitting on an unreleased interview with Tupac Shakur conducted shortly before his death in 1996. Now, 30 years later, she’s ready to pull back the curtain with a four-part podcast on Netflix where she plays the tapes for contemporary hip-hop luminaries like Joe Budden, Charlamagne and Big Boy, as well as figures more directly related to the events in question, like Outlawz member Edi I Mean or Biggie’s right-hand-man Lil Cease.

It has been revealed that as the story goes: Pac became a fan of Angie and her work while incarcerated in Upcoming York, so much so that after his release he invited her to appear in the music video for his song “I Ain’t Mad at Cha.” Angie refused, and when Pac asked why she explained that a figure so closely associated with the New York rap scene appearing in that video as East Coast-West Coast tensions reached a boiling point could only be a bad look. Pac then invited her to his home to air it all out. So the Voice of New York spent over two hours with Pac hoping to come back with an interview that defused any negative energy. What she got instead was a Pac at his most turnt, angry, hurt, and vengeful, with the rapper saying things about Significant, Puffy, and other New York rappers that would’ve only escalated those tensions. So Martinez sat on them, until today.

After viewing all four episodes of the podcast, I connected with Angie to find out why this was the right moment to release the interview, how she assembled such an all-star team of contributors, what she makes of the backlash to her decision, and how the The Tupac Tapes might help our fractured media landscape today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so blueprint ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

According to recent reports, make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Recent findings suggest that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Industry observers note that place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

In a recent development, do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.
