Industry observers note that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he prepares to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul at the moment chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

The move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

In a recent development, murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul stated in a press release that he plans to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”.

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote.

Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

According to recent reports, lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he stated, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”.

It has been revealed that but he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”.

Industry observers note that lankford stated he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”.

Here, five surprisingly “now” ways to wear the ankle boots of “then”.

The most popular ankle boots of the 2010s were those with a sole jacked far above the ground. See: anything Jeffrey Campbell produced, which usually came studded within an inch of their lives. Sienna Miller con minifalda de jean.

A longstanding fashion archetype, biker boots are rarely not “in”, but have enjoyed a resurgence in recent seasons thanks, in large part, to Miu Miu’s buckled suede iterations. Worn with skinny jeans and a shrunken leather jacket à la Gisele Bündchen, the look is as much a fixture of the AllSaints shop floor in 2026 as it was in 2016.

Recent findings suggest that if anyone could make a convincing case for the surprising chicness of a suede ankle boot, it’s Kate Moss–who, in fairness, could make a convincing case for the surprising chicness of just about anything. Here she is wearing Alaïa’s corset-laced booties on a trip to Boots, of all places, with a close-cut military tweed jacket that feels particularly of today’s moment.

Hear me out: high-shine patent booties worn not in an “I’m going to the club because I just got my A-level results in 2010” way, but in a Mary-Kate Olsen attending the Burberry Prorsum (RIP) autumn/winter 2010 show way. The addition of don’t-look-at-me sunglasses and a caped wool coat lends the look that evil fashion editor quality to which we all—or at least I—aspire.

In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that with only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished.
  • Sources indicate that the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder.
  • In a recent development, what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman notes. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

Sources indicate that the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, claims of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

In a recent development, what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman notes. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she says.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up promptly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

It has been revealed that boasting a brief ingredient list and a short cooking time, this easy chicken dish is one you’ll be making all season. Basic butter becomes the star here—it turns brown and nutty, then gets infused with sage and garlic for a savory sauce that’s basted over simply seasoned chicken breasts. A big squeeze of lemon, plus its zest, helps balance the richness. This skillet dinner is perfect for a speedy weeknight meal, but it’s also special enough for organization.

The protein:You don’t have to limit yourself to chicken here. Feel free to replace the breasts with pork chops, shrimp, scallops, or skinless salmon or halibut fillets. Simply adjust the cooking time to properly cook the protein, but be sure to maintain a medium heat. While meat and fish are often cooked on medium-high heat for a nice char, it needs to be a bit lower to avoid bitter residue in the pan, since the butter will be browned immediately afterward.

The crunch:The sage leaves crisp while the butter browns, but there are also ways to add more texture. Stirring in a handful of slivered almonds toward the end of cooking adds to the nuttiness of the dish; pine nuts, pistachios, or roughly chopped walnuts would also work. If you have a container of them, feel free to sprinkle some fried onions on top tableside.

Industry observers note that storage and serving ideas:This is not a make-ahead situation; it should be eaten immediately after it’s cooked. Serve with a simple salad dressed in a light vinaigrette to balance the richness. To soak up the sauce, mashed potatoes—traditional or sweet—are ideal. Or, to add another nutty element, roast some Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, or butternut squash to eat alongside and round out the meal.

Recent findings suggest that whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

According to recent reports, turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

It has been revealed that when dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

According to recent reports, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Sources indicate that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

In a recent development, bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

Industry observers note that while the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

It has been revealed that make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

Industry observers note that when the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

In a recent development, “I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

Industry observers note that that majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

According to recent reports, republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

In a recent development, colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

It has been revealed that “I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I mentioned, ‘You got to run,’” the Upcoming York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of Upcoming Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

In a recent development, colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” claims a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

It has been revealed that major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

It has been revealed that the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

It has been revealed that pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

According to recent reports, bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, puig has entered into an agreement to acquire Parfums de Marly and its sister brand, Initio, the Spanish beauty and fashion conglomerate announced on Friday. Advent International, the private equity firm that acquired them in 2023, sold its 75% stake in Artessence Group, the holding entity behind Parfums de Marly and Initio Parfums Privés, to Puig for €1.2 billion in cash.

“Niche fragrances offer one of the most attractive opportunities within our core fragrance business,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa remarked in a statement. “Parfums de Marly brings meaningful growth and an established position in North America, while Initio is a distinctive brand with significant potential ahead. We look forward to welcoming Julien and the Artessence team to Puig and building alongside them.”.

Julien Sprecher founded Parfums de Marly in 2009, inspired by his passion “for the splendor of the French art de vivre in the 18th century”. He sold a majority stake to Advent in 2023, remaining creative director of Parfums de Marly and minority shareholder of the group. Patrice Béliard joined Artessence in October 2025 from The Estée Lauder Companies, taking on the CEO role. Today, Parfums de Marly counts around 25 stores and 1,000 points of sale globally.

Artessence is expected to generate around $420-440 million in revenues and around $180-190 million in EBITDA in the fiscal year 2026-27, ending March 31, 2027, according to the press release.

In a recent development, at its Capital Markets Day in October, Puig signaled its openness to pursuing external growth opportunities. “We count on M&A to accelerate our growth,” Albesa stated. The group also revealed a new set of objectives that includes scaling its niche fragrances (Byredo, Penhaligon’s, L’Artisan Parfumeur and Dries Van Noten). “Niche is no longer niche,” Thomas James, president of niche brands and wellness brands at Puig, said.

In a recent development, albesa added in Friday’s statement: “Together with our other niche houses, [Parfums de Marly and Initio] give us a stronger platform from which to accelerate our ambition in the category, and we look forward to supporting the continued growth of each fragrance house, while preserving the creativity and uniqueness of each of our brands. This transaction will reinforce our core business and is fully aligned with our Vision 2032 ambition to scale what works profitably.”.

Sources indicate that puig and a holding structure established by Sprecher have agreed to an earn-out based on Artessence’s future performance, as well as put and call options over Julien Sprecher’s remaining 25% stake, providing a pathway for Puig to own 100% of the company over time. “Puig shares our belief in the power of distinctive brands and long-term brand building,” Sprecher said. “I am delighted to have the opportunity to continue this journey with a family company that understands fragrance deeply and respects the entrepreneurial and creative culture that has brought us this far.”.

Puig executive chairman Marc Puig stated: “This transaction reflects our selective approach to M&A: we invest in attractive brands with a strong strategic fit that complement our organic growth, while preserving our financial flexibility.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

Sources indicate that more difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

Latest in this patch: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

It has been revealed that food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

Industry observers note that there are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor problem is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

It has been revealed that the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Good Grips 3-Piece Silicone Utensil Set.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes.

According to recent reports, what we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

According to recent reports, what we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No.

According to recent reports, what we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

Industry observers note that once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

If crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

If steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

It has been revealed that the same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

With five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That noted, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

It has been revealed that high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

Recent findings suggest that it depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

Industry observers note that not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable.
  • The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • In a recent development, it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

In a recent development, it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

Industry observers note that while this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

Sources indicate that but getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

This is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an important role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous Fresh York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Sources indicate that smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

  • President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.
  • On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the upcoming Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the upcoming Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

According to recent reports, at every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

According to recent reports, voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine stated it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality.".

Sources indicate that rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the latest Congress, stated on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he mentioned. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his latest White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine mentioned congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

It has been revealed that “Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

It has been revealed that “White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”.

Recent findings suggest that getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon indicates his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve major problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”.

According to recent reports, despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

Industry observers note that “Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”.

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”.

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Sources indicate that stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

According to recent reports, whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

It has been revealed that lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Recent findings suggest that add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

Breaking: Gravy-Braised Turkey

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment.
  • Sources indicate that this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

Sources indicate that this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

In a recent development, add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

In a recent development, nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

  • According to recent reports, the bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a lover of all veggies, I love every type of carrot out there—except packaged baby carrots. That’s right: those bright orange cylinders with suspiciously perfect rounded corners that lurk in vending machines, school lunchboxes, and convenience store cold cases across our nation. They might be easy to eat on the go and better for you than a bag of Cheetos, but there’s a lot more going on behind the scenes of this seemingly simple healthy snack.

Here’s the truth about baby carrots—and why you might want to think twice about snagging a bag.

According to recent reports, the bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size. Real baby carrots are immature carrots harvested before they reach full size. They’re sold in bunches—unpeeled, often with the tops still attached.

While a whole carrot has a delicate, nuanced sweetness, the taste of these so-called baby carrots is best described as... factory-fresh. Don’t believe me? Grab a bag of regular carrots and do a side-by-side taste test.

Baby carrots were originally “invented” in the 1980s to make misshapen or broken carrots sellable. This was a smart way to reduce food waste and save money, but it also helped reinforce the unrealistic expectation that produce must look perfect in order to taste good. Today, baby-cut carrots are grown and processed to meet specific standards for size and shape, all to produce those identical little orange cylinders.

Here’s the bottom line: When you buy a bag of baby carrots, you’re buying into a world that’s seemingly as obsessed with unnatural perfection as the modern-day beauty industry.

In a recent development, energy conservation is top of mind for consumers these days, but making baby carrots look so uniform takes a lot of machinery. After they’re sorted, they chop the carrots into roughly 2-inch pieces and shave them—twice. Then, they go through a rough cutter, which gives them a general shape, before being polished to create those unrealistically perfect rounded edges. That’s a lot of extra work to make something that was completely edible to begin with look a certain way.

Industry observers note that to prevent bacterial growth, baby carrots may be rinsed with a diluted chlorine solution before packaging. They’re then rinsed with water, and the chlorine treatment itself is an “acceptable” food-safety practice which doesn’t make baby carrots unsafe to eat. Still, do you really want your “fresh” snack to have undergone chlorine treatments of any kind? For me, that’s a hard no, and I’d rather buy whole carrots and wash and cut them myself.

In a recent development, because baby carrots have been peeled and cut, they're more prone to drying out and developing something called “carrot blush,” a thin white film caused by dehydration. The film itself is harmless, but it certainly doesn’t make them look appetizing. Worse, they can turn slimy inside the bag, even before you open it. And that’s downright gross.

According to recent reports, prices vary depending on where you shop, but baby-cut carrots can cost more per pound than regular whole carrots. You're essentially paying extra for someone else to handle the peeling, cutting, and polishing. For a task that takes barely any time at home, I'd rather keep the difference in my wallet.

Seriously. Enjoy the taste and texture of whole carrots, potentially save some money, and skip the extra processing by simply buying a bag of whole carrots and cutting them yourself. It’ll take you less time than you spent reading this article.

For a home buzz cut, a set of guards that stay put and are easy to tell apart can matter more than the extra adjustments you’d find on a barber’s clipper. For fades and lineups, blade control and visibility matter more.

Adam Hurly’s years of testing clippers at home and speaking with barbers underpin this guide. What is the best hair clipper for men, according to GQ?

In a recent development, the best men’s hair clipper for most people is Wahl’s Color Pro Cordless for its intuitive use and low cost. As we say at GQ, most people shouldn’t be giving themselves a fancy haircut. So if you require more than a simple buzz, visit the pros.

According to recent reports, beard trimmer vs. hair clippers: What’s the difference?

While many devices can be used as both beard trimmers and hair clippers, these devices differ in their approach to hair cutting: Beard trimmers typically require less power (since facial hair tends to be less dense) but also more precision on the average device. Meanwhile, hair clippers require more muscle to mow through thicker patches of hair, and the pros will use additional detailing devices for any fancy edgework. Also, beard trimmers are often waterproof, while hair clippers are less likely to be so.

What does zero gap mean with hair clippers?

Think of zero gapping as the ability to get an actual skin-tight clip from your hair clippers. This is done by a slight realignment of the blades so that the hairs can reach right up to those teeth. It’s usually only found on professional clippers and should be left to the pros, given the risks of cutting your skin so close to the blade. (We repeat: Proceed with caution.).

Sources indicate that it’s best to let a professional barber or stylist fade your hair, however the general logic behind fading is to steadily decrease the clipper length (starting with a low trim or bare shave at the perimeter). If you insist on doing this yourself, then read GQ’s guide to fading your own hair.

Are hair clippers allowed on airplanes?

Yes, your hair clippers are allowed on the airplane, but only in your carry-on hand baggage. Nothing with fixed batteries can be checked in the cargo.

Jovan Figueroa is a barber and hair stylist and serves as a brand ambassador for STMNT Grooming Goods.

JoAnn Noriega is a San Francisco-based barber at Headprint Studio.

It has been revealed that introduced in 2014, Nespresso’s Vertuoline modernized the brand’s original pressure brew method and marked the true beginning of Nespresso espresso and coffee machines. Most Vertuo machines feature just one button and brew both coffee and espresso-style shots using a centrifugal method. Once you choose your preferred pod based on style, roast, and cup size, the machine takes care of the rest. That’s because the rim of every dome-shaped Vertuo capsule features a barcode that tells the Nespresso Vertuo machine how much water and what extraction speed to use for each pod—and can brew everything from a single and double espresso shot to a 14-ounce cup of coffee. The very first Vertuo machine released more than a decade ago is still kicking, and it's one of the best values you can get.

Vertuo Next Coffee with Aeroccino Milk Frother.

What People Are Saying:“This is my family's FAVORITE vegan pumpkin pie - we make it every year…” - GoldPaw.

The best part about this pie is that you don’t need to chill the pie dough at all. Preheat your oven to 375° and grease your pie plate.

Recent findings suggest that then, use a food processor to pulse the pecans, oats, sugar, and salt until they’re fine crumbs. Stream in the coconut oil and then pulse until the dough forms. You’re done! The easiest pie dough you’ll ever make.

Press the dough into your greased pie plate in an even layer– make sure you press the dough up the sides of the pan as well. Place parchment over the dough and fill with dried beans, rice, or pie weights. Bake for 10 minutes and then remove the parchment and bake for another 10 minutes.

Sources indicate that to make the filling, whisk all of the filling ingredients together in a large bowl. Pour it into the par-baked crust, smoothing the top.

Bake the pie in the oven for 50 to 55 minutes. If the crust starts to get too dark, cover the whole pie with foil. You’ll know the pie is done when it looks set and dry on top but is still slightly jiggly in the center. Let cool in the refrigerator before serving with some whipped topping alongside.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

According to recent reports, keep your pie in the fridge for up to 4 days, loosely covered with foil. Keep the whipped cream separate and dollop onto each pie slice as you serve. If the whipped cream loses structure, keep it cold and re-whip with a handheld mixer as needed.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any latest bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

In a recent development, the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., remarked in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

Recent findings suggest that “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

According to recent reports, the Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura stated his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Sources indicate that jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He stated that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, stated that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He stated the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A fresh Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

It has been revealed that congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

Industry observers note that the House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

In a recent development, honestly, we can’t think of anything better than a galette. Industry observers note that arrange the apple slices on top of the dough in alternating rows, leaving about a 1 ½” border around the edge. Then, fold the dough edge nearest to you toward the center and rotate the baking sheet, repeating this step until all 4 edges of the dough are folded in toward the fruit.

Remove the galette from the oven and transfer it to a cooling rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

A galette is essentially an open-faced pie. Thinly sliced apples are tossed in cinnamon and sugar and layered on top of a single sheet of pie crust. The crust is folded over the apples in a rough circle and baked until the crust is flaky. Apple pie has a top and bottom crust and is usually formed in a pie dish. The extra crust and overall shape are the only real differences, and for the apple obsessed, galettes provide the perfect ratio of crust to filling.

It has been revealed that anything you'd serve with an apple pie would work here as well. That means your favorite ice cream, frozen yogurt, caramel sauce, or candied nuts would be great galette sidekicks.

Any leftover galette can be stored for up to 4 days in the refrigerator.

In a recent development, in my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table. If you’re looking to take the classic from good to million-dollar-price-tag-worthy, then this is the recipe for you. My million-dollar mac & cheese is what happens when you decide to take basic mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy, crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food will take center stage on any table it hits.

According to recent reports, the cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese. For this million-dollar mac, I chose Pecorino Romano as my accent, but went slightly rogue with the other two and paired fontina and French raclette, which both melt well and have quite a bit of funk. French raclette is particularly great for a mac & cheese sauce since it becomes almost fondue-like when melted, giving you cheese pulls beyond your wildest dreams.

The combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac. That mentioned, if you absolutely can’t find them, you could try combining comté and Camembert or Gruyère and brie with the Pecorino to give you a similar result.

Recent findings suggest that the crispy topping:With a dish as rich and creamy as this mac & cheese, a crispy, crunchy topping is key. Pre-toasting the panko in butter on the stove ensures a truly golden-brown, delicious topping, without the nail-biting broiler-watching session. Using a higher butter-fat European-style butter here (as well as in the sauce) brings additional richness, ensuring this million-dollar mac is as decadent as it should be. In testing, I found that the breadcrumbs on top of the mac didn’t brown much more when they were on top of the mac in the oven, but if you’re concerned about them getting too dark, you can always lightly tent the pan with foil.

Recent findings suggest that the gold leaf topping is a fun way to cue the whole “million-dollar” thing, but it’s totally not necessary. Use it if you want, but don’t feel obligated!

Storage:Any leftover mac & cheese can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave, covered, in 30-second bursts until warmed through or, if you have enough, in the oven in a covered ceramic dish.
