📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no exaggeration to say that xawaash is at the heart of Somali cuisine. It is Somali history on a plate—a culinary reminder of Somalia’s centuries of global trade, particularly along the Indian Ocean. Xawaash is what makes many Somali dishes taste distinctly Somali. While every household’s xawaash recipe is its own, typically seven core spices—cumin, coriander, black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and turmeric—are toasted until their fragrance blooms, then blended into an earthy golden-brown powder. Xawaash stores very well and for a long time in an airtight container, though it’s at its peak shortly after it’s made. If you use it often, you can double or triple the recipe for a big batch.

Like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar. It has a hint of heat thanks to the black pepper and optional jalapeño. Suqaar is cooked covered to keep the meat juicy and moist. Serve with the flatbread of your choice (canjeero, muufo, or sabaayad) for a light lunch or over plenty of rice for a more filling dinner.

More tasty chicken thigh recipes here.

It has been revealed that toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp. green cardamom pods, and 1½ tsp. whole cloves in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly so the spices don’t burn. The spices are toasted when they have a slightly darker color and become fragrant, 1–2 minutes. Transfer the toasted spices to a blender or spice grinder and blend until they become a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and mix in ¼ cup (30 g) ground turmeric until it’s fully incorporated and the spice mix is golden brown. Allow to cool completely, then store in an airtight container.

It has been revealed that in a medium bowl, combine the juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp. xawaash, 1 tsp. fine sea salt, ½ tsp. paprika, and ⅛ tsp. ground black pepper. Add 1 lb. (450 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-sized pieces, and mix everything together to coat the chicken. Set aside.

In a large skillet over medium-high heat, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil until loose. Add 1 large yellow onion, halved and sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes, or until the onion is softened. Add 6 garlic cloves, minced, and 1 medium jalapeño, halved, and stir for another minute, then add the chicken in a single layer. Allow it to cook undisturbed for 5 minutes, then turn the pieces over and cook for 3 minutes more, until fully cooked through.

Add the remaining 1½ tsp. xawaash, ¾ cup (12 g) coarsely chopped cilantro leaves, 1 medium red bell pepper, sliced, and 1 medium yellow bell pepper, sliced, and stir to combine. Cover the skillet and turn the heat down to medium-low; cook until the peppers have softened, 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot.

Want to treat yourself to five-star brunch without making a ton of dishes—or taking off your pj’s? Hack the classic croque madame by making it in the air fryer. Here, crispy toast is topped with an egg and smothered with ham, cheese, and béchamel for a simpler version of the classic French dish that will transform the comfort of your sofa into a fancy brunch spot in five seconds flat.

Sources indicate that how is this a croque madame?A classic croque madame is a toasted ham and cheese sandwich that’s topped with a layer of béchamel, broiled until bubbly, and then topped with a fried egg. This air fryer version takes all those components—toasty bread, fried egg, béchamel, ham, and cheese—and reconfigures them into a form that cooks much easier in the air fryer. You might say it almost looks like a classic egg-in-the-hole, but don’t worry! If you close your eyes, you’ll still taste croque madame.

Sources indicate that the microwave béchamel:There’s nothing wrong with making béchamel in a pot on the stove, but making it in the microwave means fewer heavy dishes to clean—and it’s also a great hack to know if you’re somewhere with limited (or no!) stove space. Rather than standing over a pot, whisking constantly, you’ll simply whisk the flour into the melted butter, microwave until it’s bubbling, then whisk in the milk and microwave again. Once it’s thickened, you can fold in the cheese. Though I don’t recommend microwaving after the cheese goes in—that’s a sure way to break your sauce—if it absolutely needs it, you can microwave it for very short bursts just till it melts together.

Delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

Sources indicate that make-ahead & storage:Once cooked, the air fryer croque madame should be eaten immediately. That mentioned, the béchamel can be made 2 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator. I recommend gently reheating it before using. I typically do this in the microwave in 15-second increments, stirring in between—this prevents the sauce from breaking.

BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Industry observers note that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Sources indicate that add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

Breaking: Why ‘Blackout Wednesday’ Has Become One Of The Biggest Drinking Nights Of The Year

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (459 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delish editors handpick every product we feature.
  • Wednesday isn’t typically a massive night for restaurants and bars—but the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is different.
  • That’s how Thanksgiving Eve came to be known as “Blackout Wednesday” or “Drinksgiving,” one of the busiest drinking nights of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Wednesday isn’t typically a massive night for restaurants and bars—but the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is different. Most people have the next day off, and college students or young professionals are typically back in their hometowns for the holiday. What better way to kick off the long weekend than to get off your parents’ couch and hit up the local watering hole?

That’s how Thanksgiving Eve came to be known as “Blackout Wednesday” or “Drinksgiving,” one of the busiest drinking nights of the year. A 2023 study found that in 2022, liquor sales grew by 156% and beer sales increased by 85% on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Cocktail orders surged by 69%.

Recent findings suggest that doorDash has even named the day one of the busiest for alcohol deliveries. Among 10 more traditional holidays like New Year’s Eve and July 4th, Blackout Wednesday ranks right in the middle. “As families and friends return home for the winter holidays, the day before Thanksgiving has become the fifth most popular day for alcohol delivery,” DoorDash’s website reads.

According to recent reports, going out in your hometown is prime time for idly snooping on people from high school, witnessing some truly unlikely pairings (Tyler and Kayla?!). It’s social and nostalgic, but it’s also a day when one drink can easily turn into one too many.

It’s not all fun and drinking games, however. This unofficial holiday marks the start of so-called “DUI Season,” with checkpoints ramping up before Turkey Day. Your risk of coming into contact with a drunk driver also becomes 55% higher than on average days.

Short-term risks of heavy drinking and blacking out include vomiting, seizures, depression, and accidental injuries, as well as next-day anxiety and depression. Long-term, recurring binges are linked to liver damage, high blood pressure, and mental health issues. Alcohol-induced blackouts can also occur more rapidly after just a few drinks, especially if you are taking certain medications, drink on an empty stomach, or have a low body weight.

It’s totally valid to blow off some steam (or get out of chopping celery), just plan it smart. With actually-delicious mocktails, non-alcoholic beers, and ride-shares, there’s very little reason to put yourself—or others—in danger, especially during the holidays.

Hosts and guests alike can benefit from making a plan for keeping everyone safe until well after Latest Year’s Day by providing plenty of non-alcoholic options at gatherings, opting in on a “Dampsgiving,” checking in with loved ones (and designated drivers) before they hit the road, and always making sure there’s a spot on the couch for anyone who helped themselves to a few too many eggnog espresso martinis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again: Every holiday table needs a salad. This one was dreamed up for Hanukkah, my family’s second-favorite special occasion after Thanksgiving. Serve it with roast chicken or salmon and you have an objectively perfect meal. It’s bright, crunchy, and decked out with little “latkes.” Potato croutons have popped up in a few places over the years, like The Salad Lab’s own Hanukkah-inspired salad (great minds!), Daniel Humm’s salmon rösti salad from Made Nice, and Ore-Ida’s cutely named CrouTots. My take is as lazy as it gets: frozen tater tots, smashed. The result is ultra-crisp, like the tiniest potato pancake in the world. A salad spinner is a godsend for washing the lettuce and herbs. Any type of apple works (I like Honeycrisp or Fuji) and the fresh horseradish on top is optional. But if you can find it, get it!

More festive Hanukkah recipes this way.

Industry observers note that preheat oven to 425°. Mix together ½ cup sour cream, 3 Tbsp. drained prepared horseradish, 1 Tbsp. distilled white vinegar, a significant pinch of kosher salt, and 1 tsp. water in a small bowl, adding more water a little at a time if needed until dressing it drizzle-able. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Industry observers note that bake 1 lb. frozen tater tots on a large rimmed baking sheet for half the time of package directions (about 10 minutes).

It has been revealed that meanwhile, place 1 small white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, in a small bowl; pour in cold water to cover and add a few ice cubes. Set onions aside.

Industry observers note that tear pull apart leaves from 1 lb. romaine lettuce (about ⅔ head) and/or Little Gem lettuce (4–5 heads) and tear large leaves in half. Place in a large bowl. Remove tough stems from 1 bunch dill and 1 bunch parsley; discard. Coarsely tear remaining leaves and tender stems. Add to lettuce.

Remove tater tots from oven and, using oven mitts for safety, lay another baking sheet directly on top; firmly press down on tots to flatten. (If you don’t have a second baking sheet, use a heatproof measuring cup or mug instead.) Return tater tots to oven and bake until deep golden brown and crisp, 10–20 minutes.(If your oven has a convection setting, now is a great time to use it.).

Drain reserved onion and pat dry. Thinly slice 2 large apples (about 1 lb.). Add both to bowl with lettuce and herbs.

Drizzle 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and add a big pinch of flaky sea salt. Toss to combine, then mound salad on a platter. Evenly scatter tater tots and ¾ cup pomegranate seeds over.

Serve salad with remaining dressing for drizzling over and peeled fresh horseradish (if using) for grating over.

#170397. Latest Update: White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (824 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps.
  • It has been revealed that somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice.
  • The color comes down to a protein called myoglobin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps. There's Team White Meat, politely asking for "just a slice of breast, please." Then there's Team Dark Meat, already eyeing the drumstick like it's the last Pop-Tart in the box. It's basically Team Edward vs. Team Jacob, but with gravy.

It has been revealed that somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice. As a dietitian, I get asked about this a lot, especially the week of Thanksgiving. The short answer is that dark meat isn't the villain it's made out to be. The long answer is way more interesting, so grab a fork. Cranberry sauce optional.

The color comes down to a protein called myoglobin. Myoglobin stores oxygen inside muscle cells, and muscles that work steadily over long periods need more of it. On a turkey, that means the legs and thighs, which the bird uses to stand and walk around all day.

Recent findings suggest that domestic turkeys use their breast muscles far less, so they carry less myoglobin and stay pale. Myoglobin contains heme iron, which matters for nutrition. More on that in a minute.

According to recent reports, so when you choose dark meat, you're eating hardworking muscle. That changes its nutritional profile in a few notable ways.

Both cuts are excellent sources of protein. A 3-ounce serving of roasted, skinless turkey provides roughly 24 to 25 grams of protein, whether it's white or dark meat. White meat edges ahead by a gram or two, but in practical terms, both will do the job.

If protein is a priority, either cut gets you there. No need to stage a dramatic family intervention over the drumsticks.

Recent findings suggest that skinless dark meat does have more fat than skinless white meat, typically a few extra grams per 3-ounce serving. Some of that is saturated fat.

Context matters, though. The difference amounts to a few grams on a single plate, not a massive gap. Keeping the skin on also adds more fat to either cut. A slice of breast with crispy skin can end up in a similar ballpark to skinless thigh meat.

Sources indicate that saturated fat and heart health remain an active area of research. A Cochrane systematic review found that reducing dietary saturated fat was linked to a modest reduction in cardiovascular events over time. That finding reflects overall eating patterns across months and years, though, not what you eat at one holiday meal. A few extra grams of fat from turkey thighs won't make or break anyone's health.

Fat also brings flavor and moisture, which is why dark meat rarely turns into the dry, sawdust situation that can happen to an overcooked breast.

Remember myoglobin? Thanks in part to its heme iron, dark meat generally contains more iron than white meat. Heme iron, the type found in animal foods, is generally absorbed more efficiently than the non-heme iron found in plants.

Recent findings suggest that that's meaningful, because iron deficiency is the most common cause of anemia worldwide. It's especially common among people who menstruate, pregnant people, and young children. Turkey thighs won't fix a deficiency on their own, but they can absolutely contribute to your overall iron intake.

Sources indicate that dark meat also delivers noticeably more zinc than white meat. Zinc plays a key role in immune function, wound healing, and taste perception. Not bad for the part of the bird some people skip.

This is where things get fun, because each cut has its own nutritional strengths.

These B vitamins help your body turn food into usable energy. Vitamin B12 also supports nerve function and red blood cell production, and B12 deficiency is more common in older adults and people who eat few animal foods.

Neither cut offers a complete B vitamin package on its own. Together, though? They make a pretty great team.

In a recent development, not really. It's just different. White meat offers slightly more protein and less fat, plus more niacin and B6. Dark meat has more iron, zinc, and riboflavin, plus richer flavor and a juicier texture. Both provide vitamin B12.

Neither one deserves a "good" or "bad" label. Health is shaped by your eating patterns over time, not by which slice you pick from the platter on one Thursday in November.

If you have a specific health condition, a registered dietitian can help you figure out what works best for you. For most people, though, the best turkey is the one you actually enjoy eating.

In a recent development, pick the cut you love. Better yet, take a little of both. Dark meat isn't a nutritional compromise, and white meat isn't a punishment. They're two parts of the same bird, each with its own strengths.

So go ahead and claim that drumstick. Or the breast. Or both. Your plate, your call. Just save some gravy for the rest of us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one pot, four hits of lemon: Juice (limone #1) and zest (limone #2) in the cooking water, then more juice (limone #3) and zest (limone #4) to ﬁnish. The contrast of cooked and fresh citrus yields a lemon experience as wild as it gets—at least as far as pasta goes. Crème fraîche and Parmigiano-Reggiano mellow the acid into submission, delivering a creamy yet punchy ﬁnal product just begging for forks… and maybe one more squeeze of lemon.

Want some protein here? Add one pound of peeled and deveined medium shrimp to the pot as soon as the pasta turns uncomfortably al dente.

More puckery, lemony dishes this way.

It has been revealed that remove the zest from 2 lemons with a vegetable peeler in long, lengthwise strips. Chop the strips very fine. (You should have a heaping 2 Tbsp.) Transfer half the chopped zest to a large pot or Dutch oven. Reserve the remaining half.

Squeeze enough juice from the lemons to measure ½ cup (120 ml); reserve the remaining lemon for squeezing at the finish. Transfer ¼ cup (60 ml) of the juice to the pot with the zest and reserve the remaining juice for serving. Add 3½ cups (840 ml) water, 1 large shallot, peeled and thinly sliced, 2 Tbsp. (30 g) unsalted butter, 4 thyme sprigs, leaves stripped and stems discarded, and 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt.

According to recent reports, place the pot over high heat and bring to a boil. Add 1 lb. (454 g) egg noodles. (Don’t worry if they’re not fully submerged.) Cook, stirring, until the pasta is uncomfortably al dente, 5–7 minutes. Reduce the heat to medium to maintain a lively but gentle simmer and add 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and ¼ cup (60 ml) water, stirring to incorporate and create a pan sauce. Continue cooking and adding water, ¼ cup (60 ml) at a time, until there is a generous amount of sauce pooling in the pot and the noodles are al dente, 3–5 minutes more. Add ⅓ cup (80 g) crème fraîche, the remaining finely chopped lemon zest, and the reserved ¼ cup (60 ml) lemon juice. Season with kosher salt and taste. If the only flavor you’re getting is lemon, continue salting to bring out the creaminess.

Serve topped with a big dollop of crème fraîche and a squeeze of lemon juice. Shower with the remaining 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and pinches of flaky sea salt. (Yes, this is a lot of Parm! But stay with me here… it’s a vital balance to the punches of lemon.) Top with more thyme leaves, and if desired, cracked black pepper and chopped roasted hazelnuts.

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Industry observers note that vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

Recent findings suggest that "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night.".

Trump has noted that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

According to recent reports, the situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Industry observers note that trump, Vance and other administration officials have remarked in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

It has been revealed that republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly.".

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

Recent findings suggest that “With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Recent findings suggest that asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.

In a recent development, if your holiday spread always includes a plate of crispy latkes and a round of dirty martinis, these dirty martini latkes are probably your dream mash-up. This playful party app takes everything you love about the classic Hanukkah potato pancake and gives it a cocktail-inspired twist with buttery green olives, pimento peppers, and a tangy blue cheese and vermouth-spiked sour cream for dipping. The blue cheese isn’t mandatory, but if you love an ice-cold filthy martini with a couple of blue cheese stuffed olives in it, you’ll totally understand my vision. Pair these with other Hanukkah favorites for a festive spread that's equal parts nostalgic and fun.

The latkes:Traditional latkes start with freshly grated potatoes, but frozen shredded hash browns are the secret shortcut here, cutting prep time without sacrificing crispy edges or fluffy centers. The key is squeezing out as much moisture as possible, then fluffing the shreds with a fork so they stay light instead of turning dense. Castelvetrano olives add a rich, buttery flavor, but Spanish queen or manzanilla olives work just as well. If you can find green olives already stuffed with pimento, go ahead and use them—you can skip the extra chopped pimentos altogether.

Make ahead & storage:The vermouth-blue cheese dipping sauce can be made up to 7 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, making your day-of party prep that much easier. Leftover latkes can be refrigerated for up to 4 days; just reheat them in a 400° oven or air fryer until hot and crisp again for the best texture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I’ve always loved Italian American food. Maybe because Italian and Korean cooking have traits in common: Both are homey and resourceful, and grandmothers are revered for their signature dishes made without formal recipes. This recipe was one of the first Korean Italian fusion recipes I developed, and it makes use of my two favorite secret weapons: kimchi and fish sauce. The result is the Bolognese you know and love, but with a deep, tangy twist. Fish sauce in Italian cooking is not a fresh idea, actually—Romans have been using salted anchovies and garum, an ancient kind of fish sauce, for centuries. For an extra-special finish, I love garnishing this with baek (white) kimchi for acidity. But it’s optional, and regular kimchi (or no kimchi) works just fine, too.

More winning pasta recipes this way.

Recent findings suggest that start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 medium-yellow onion, finely diced (about 1½ cups), 2 carrots, peeled and finely diced, and 3 stalks celery, finely diced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and the edges start to brown, about 4 minutes. Stir in 4 cloves garlic, minced, and a pinch of kosher salt and cook for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup chopped kimchi and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook until the kimchi pieces start to soften, about 3 minutes. Pour in ½ cup red wine, increase the heat, and simmer, stirring with a wooden spoon to dislodge any bits that have stuck to the bottom, until the wine has nearly disappeared, about 2 minutes.

Sources indicate that add the meat: Stir in 1 lb. ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.

Add the tomatoes: Pour one 28-oz. can whole San Marzano tomatoes in a bowl. Using clean hands, squish the tomatoes into small pieces. Pour the tomatoes into the pot and add 1 cup beef broth or water, ½ tsp. dried Italian seasoning or dried oregano, a pinch of salt, and a few grinds of freshly ground black pepper. Bring to a simmer and lower the heat to medium-low. Gently cook, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is just thick enough to stand up on a spoon, about 20 minutes. Stir in 2 Tbsp. fish sauce and taste, then add more salt or fish sauce if needed.

Cook the noodles and serve: In a pot of boiling salted water, cook 1 lb. spaghetti according to package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until al dente. Drain the noodles in a colander, then give the colander a shake to get rid of extra water. Divide the noodles among serving plates and spoon the Bolognese on top. Garnish with 1 cup chopped kimchi (white or regular; if using) and 2 Tbsp. chopped flat-leaf parsley and serve.

Do Ahead: Leftover Bolognese sauce (without the noodles) keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or in the freezer for up to 2 months.

There’s an Actual Holiday for Eating Thanksgiving Leftovers Over the Kitchen Sink

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (431 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s the morning after Thanksgiving.
  • Sources indicate that as it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.

Recent findings suggest that it’s the morning after Thanksgiving. The good dishes are still drying, the fridge is a Tetris board of foil-wrapped leftovers and you’re standing over the kitchen sink eating cold stuffing with your bare hands. No plate, no judgment.

Sources indicate that as it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience. It’s called Sinkie Day, and it’s been around since long before TikTok made girl dinner a thing.

Industry observers note that for that, we have Norm Hankoff to thank. An advertising consultant from California, he had his lightbulb moment in 1991 “while wolfing down some tuna salad over his sink, using extra-strength potato chips as utensils,” according to a 1997 Associated Press report.

Convinced he couldn’t be the only one, Hankoff founded the International Association of People Who Dine Over the Kitchen Sink and declared the day after Thanksgiving Sinkie Day. By 1997, more than 1,000 people had joined, and each one received a membership certificate stamped with a double sink and the group’s motto: “Everybody does it. Sinkies proudly admit it.”.

Naturally, there was a cookbook—or rather, a don’t-cook book. Published by a tech giant cheekily called Digester’s Reader, The Official Sinkies Don’t Cook Book included such culinary masterpieces as “cakeless frosting” and “meat loaf in your fist.” Other recipes called for little more than a handful of mashed potatoes or a piece of chocolate cake dunked in a glass of milk.

Hankoff even set his sights on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. When Hillary Clinton was looking for a chef in 1994, he sent her a copy of his book and suggested the first family give sink-side snacking a try. No word on whether they took his advice, but the White House did send him a thank-you letter.

According to recent reports, the beauty of Sinkie Day, which falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, is that it’s perhaps the only food holiday that actively encourages you to do less. A fridge full of Thanksgiving extras is all it takes, though a few upgrades never hurt:.

Recent findings suggest that of course, a holiday devoted to leftovers is also a good excuse to brush up on food safety. As long as everything hit the fridge within two hours of cooking, you’ve got three to four days to work your way through it.

It has been revealed that whether you're hosting a small gathering this year or simply craving the comforting flavors of Thanksgiving any time of year, this sheet-pan dinner is the way to go. It’s a feast that’s as cozy as it is convenient, bringing together the classics with a few flavorful twists. The beauty of this meal lies in its simplicity—everything roasts together on a single pan, making cleanup a breeze.

The turkey:Using a bone-in split turkey breast helps ensure juicy, flavorful meat with rich, golden skin, slathered with butter and seasoned with poultry seasoning. This nod to tradition is enhanced with a touch of smoky paprika and garlic to amp up the flavors. For the stuffing, I went the classic route, using store-bought seasoned cubes for a bit of nostalgia, along with onions, celery, and soy sauce to boost the savory notes, and cranberries for a hint of sweetness. The stuffing offers the best of both worlds, with crispy edges and an irresistibly savory center soaked in turkey drippings.

It has been revealed that the sweet potatoes:The sweet potatoes strike a perfect balance, spiced with warm and aromatic garam masala—a perfect pairing with the sweet yet earthy tuber. A splash of orange juice adds a tart-sweet touch, while pecans provide a satisfying crunch. If garam masala isn’t your thing, a dash of pumpkin pie spice works beautifully.

The green beans:The green beans, a nod to the iconic casserole, are streamlined for the sheet pan, tossed with mushrooms, Parmesan, and thyme-infused butter, and finished with crispy fried onions for that quintessential touch.

Make-ahead & storage:If the idea of making a whole Thanksgiving dinner on a sheet pan in one day feels daunting, here’s a tip—prep some components ahead of time. Most, if not all, of the ingredient chopping, grating, toasting, etc., can be done 2 to 3 days in advance. The stuffing can be made a day ahead; just be sure to cool it completely before refrigerating. Even the turkey can be buttered and seasoned the day before, leaving you with just the assembly and roasting on the day of.

#170380. We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (587 w)

We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.
  • I have a particular weakness for antique dishes.
  • Sources indicate that then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Sources indicate that then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

Ellie Martin Cliffe For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, according to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

It has been revealed that moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He says that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

Recent findings suggest that for gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

This is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

In a recent development, and if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

To build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights tech giant HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

In a recent development, the Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

We’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

According to recent reports, culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the company is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In a recent development, in-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products. Between our own purchases and the endless stream of samples sent our way, it means there’s always something new coming across our desks and into our homes. Each month we round up the standouts we tested or bought ourselves that changed the way we cook and eat.

This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea.

Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November.

This summer, I spent a week in Paris with my family and gloriously found myself eating steak frites on more than one occasion. Besides the perfectly cooked bavette and thin, crisp fries, I was enamored with the bistro aesthetic—down to the super-sharp and sleek steak knives I used for each meal. When I came across Made In Cookware’s set, I knew it was a sign that I, too, could adopt this sophisticated French look. These knives are manufactured in Thiers, France, a region known for knife-making, which speaks to their aesthetic and craftsmanship. I love that they’re non-serrated; the sharp edges maintain the integrity of meat and can be sharpened once dull. These steak knives are also full tang, which means they’re constructed with a single rod of stainless steel from tip to handle. And speaking of the handle—the feature that attracted me to this set in the first place—they come in several materials, including olive wood, black polymer, and (my pick) pearlescent acetate. — Melissa Knific, contributing editor.

According to recent reports, what is a martini glass if not a tiny birdbath for my olives? These Year and Day glasses are my favorite kind: classic and elevated, but durable. They’re great for anything you’d serve up, and the best part is that I can set them in the dishwasher at the end of the night. —Casey Hendricks, executive director of audience development.

A woman in her late 20s who starts her mornings with a mug of bone broth as the weather gets cold—I know I’m a cliché. But this chicken bone broth from Fond, specifically the turmeric and black pepper variety, truly does start my day off on the right note. There’s eight grams of protein per cup, sure, but my favorite part is that it’s made without alliums (like garlic and onion) so it’s especially kind to my tummy. Instead, the broth gets its flavor from carrots, turmeric root, celery, lemon juice, cracked black pepper, and thyme. All the vegetables Fond uses are organic and they use 100% pasture-raised chicken, so it’s as close to making my own bone broth at home as I can get, without having to simmer a pot for 18 hours. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

M6HG Instant Hot Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter.

There were a couple of things happening at my house at the same time: First, my wife’s lovely and enormous collection of houseplants continued growing; second, we decided to get a water softener to fight against the notoriously hard water in my part of Latest Jersey. Those two things don’t go together well because softened water and its added sodium can be bad for plants long term. A reverse osmosis system is one way to fight against that, but we didn’t have the budget (or really the need) for a whole-home RO system, nor did we have the space under our sink for one of those. Enter Waterdrop’s countertop RO. The M6HG has an autofilling pitcher that makes plant care convenient, but it’s also turned out it’s getting more use than our fridge filter for drinking. Water comes out a chilly 48 degrees and measures precisely to 4, 8, or 16 ounces (which my kids love for some reason). It also dispenses at 77℉, 113℉ (supposedly good for baby formula), 131℉, 149℉, 167℉, 185℉ (for delicate tea), and 203℉ (for French press or pour-over coffee). Oh yeah, it’s on big sale for Black Friday. — Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

I never grew up with advent calendars, but I can totally see what the fuss is about. My family and I take such joy opening up a window of surprise every morning. Since the advent calendars in our home are usually food-related, we’ll enjoy the treat together later in the evening, with varying degrees of jostling, depending on what it is. Well, looks like the 2026 holiday season will be another one of us throwing elbows because we have our hands on BonBon’s magnificent Lighthouse Advent Calendar. No paper windows here! The cool Swedish confectionary’s calendar is actually a long tower filled with 24 individually wrapped, numbered mini bags of vegan gummies. The daily candy should be a mix of BonBon’s exclusive upcoming flavors as well as its beloved classics. I think my Swedish husband and daughter are already losing their minds (it’s only November) and I’m already fearing for our next dental visit, but it is giving this exceptionally fast holiday season a good reason to stop and appreciate a fun, sweet moment every day. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food director.

’Tis the season for...soup. My Dutch oven and I have been on a tear making favorites like white chicken chili, chicken-lentil soup, and tons of minestrone. In my attempt to “be frugal,” I’ve been bringing my soups to work for lunch in my, yes, ludicrously capacious bag, and more specifically, my 20 oz. insulated thermos by Hydroflask. It’s truly the perfect size for a lunch-appropriate portion and keeps my soup warm from morning until around 1 p.m. when it’s time to eat between meetings. It’s completely leak-proof which is crucial for a soup commute. And, it’s dishwasher safe, so when I come home after work, I can just throw it in the dishwasher to use all over again the next day. A small investment for a considerably more delightful desk lunch. —June Kim, executive editor.

Limited Edition Peppermint Mocha Barista.

I’m not really a pumpkin spice latte girl, but a peppermint mocha is a seasonal drink I can definitely get behind—so when I heard that Táche, the brand behind my favorite pistachio milk, had come out with a Peppermint Mocha flavor, I was very eager to try it. Sure enough, it was love at first sip. It tastes deeply chocolatey thanks to the addition of Dutch-processed cocoa, and has just enough peppermint flavor to feel festive and balanced without veering into toothpaste territory. I’ve been mixing it with a shot of espresso over ice to make an easy peppermint mocha latte, but to be honest with you, my favorite way to enjoy it is straight up, chilled and poured into a glass. —Alaina Chou, commerce writer.

Sources indicate that I’m often hesitant to use pre-made, packaged products when it comes to cooking. One could say I’m a bit of a control freak, but I’m not opposed to a shortcut, especially when it’s after 7 p.m. on a weeknight and I still need to get dinner on the table.

According to recent reports, enter Gymkhana Butter Masala Mild Simmer Sauce. The London-based, two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant recently rolled out a line of sauces, marinades, and chutneys inspired by its iconic dishes. I paired the butter masala sauce with cubed paneer that I promptly broiled, topped everything with fresh cilantro, and served it alongside basmati rice.

The sauce is rich, complex, and packed with flavor, yet all it requires is a quick reheat. Dinner came together in less than 30 minutes and tasted like something I’d order at a restaurant. Needless to say, I’ll be stocking up on a few more jars. —Ali Inglese, executive producer.

I’ve absolutely been loving this soothing tisane (aka herbal tea!) from La Vie tea. Produced in the French tradition—and primarily sourced directly from French gardens!—these delicate blends are all made from herbs, flowers, and spices as opposed to tea leaves. The digestion-friendly blend I’ve been enjoying is mostly ginger, fennel, and chamomile, with notes of orange and cinnamon—I’ve been parked on the couch with a huge mug of this brew after many a hearty dinner this month. I’m looking forward to dipping into the lavender-scented “Calm” blend ahead of the forthcoming hectic holiday season! —Rebecca Firkser, test kitchen editor.

Recent findings suggest that I’m a complete nut for ice cream. Regardless of the season, I’m always ready to pop a pint open for dessert (or a mid-day pick-me-up, let’s be honest). And I can say unequivocally that Graeter’s is my favorite ice cream of all time. Even Oprah agrees with me. She named it her favorite too back in 2002. And thanks to the modern miracle that is dry ice, you can have the best ice cream on the planet sent straight to your door. This option is available year-round, allowing you to pick your own flavors in packs of six or twelve pints (get the Coconut Chip if you know what’s good for you). But if you want to get in the holiday spirit, start with the Holiday Pack. It offers an assortment of seasonal flavors as well as the always in-demand, Black Raspberry Chip. Whether you’re treating yourself this year or shopping for that impossible-to-buy-for friend, this small-batch ice cream from the Buckeye State is the way to go. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy.

In a recent development, this chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling).

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Industry observers note that whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

It has been revealed that bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Sources indicate that place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Sources indicate that beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

In a recent development, place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Recent findings suggest that dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

According to recent reports, lePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent Newly introduced England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially rolled out his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

As much as I love a big, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

According to recent reports, start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, this trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

It has been revealed that I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

For the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host says dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Sources indicate that once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

In a recent development, the short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:.

In a recent development, I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a substantial breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

It has been revealed that first, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a major deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

Sources indicate that this is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really important to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

Industry observers note that and I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really important for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

💡 Key Takeaways
